items.title: Students Use of Generative AI Models for Health Information Seeking: Lessons from a Developing Country in Africa
items.abstract: This study investigated students’ use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) models for health information seeking in Nigeria. A descriptive cross-sectional survey design was adopted. Data were collected through an online questionnaire administered to students in selected universities across the six geopolitical zones of Nigeria. A total of 308 valid responses were analyzed using descriptive and inferential statistics. The findings revealed that ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Claude were the most widely used generative AI models for health information seeking. Students frequently used AI tools for obtaining immediate health information, understanding diseases and symptoms, supporting academic research, and seeking mental health and wellness information. Convenience, ease of use, quick access to information, and free availability significantly influenced usage. Although respondents moderately trusted AI-generated health information, they emphasized the need to verify such information with healthcare professionals because of concerns about misinformation, contradictory responses, and privacy risks. The study further revealed that demographic variables had no significant influence on students’ use of generative AI models. The study concluded that generative AI models have become important health information tools among students despite associated credibility and technological challenges. The study recommended AI literacy programs, information verification training, ethical AI policies, and improved internet infrastructure in Nigerian universities.

items.title: Study on AI Education and Skill Development: NEP 2020 and AI Integration
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming an important technology in transforming education and skill development. The National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 emphasizes technology-enabled learning, multidisciplinary education, vocational education, critical thinking, creativity, and the development of future-ready skills. The integration of AI into education can support these objectives by providing personalized learning, intelligent assessment, automated feedback, digital learning resources, and improved teaching and learning processes. AI can help students learn according to their individual needs, improve academic performance, and access educational resources more effectively. It can also contribute to the development of digital literacy, problem-solving, creativity, communication, and other skills required in the changing world of work. For teachers, AI can assist in lesson planning, assessment, feedback, and identifying students' learning needs, thereby improving the overall efficiency of the education system. However, the successful integration of AI also presents several challenges. These include the digital divide, unequal access to technology, inadequate digital infrastructure, data privacy and security concerns, ethical issues, limited awareness, and insufficient training among teachers and educators. Addressing these challenges is essential to ensure that AI benefits all learners equally and is used responsibly. This study examines the role of AI in education and skill development and explores its alignment with the objectives of NEP 2020. It focuses on the opportunities offered by AI, as well as the challenges involved in its implementation. The study also suggests measures such as improving digital infrastructure, providing teacher training, promoting AI awareness, ensuring data privacy, and establishing ethical guidelines for responsible AI use. Overall, the study highlights that the effective and responsible integration of AI can strengthen the objectives of NEP 2020. By combining technological innovation with inclusive and learner-centred approaches, AI can contribute to a more personalized, accessible, innovative, and future-ready education system in India. Keywords: AI Personalized learning, intelligent assessment, digital learning resources, language support, and improved teaching methods.

items.title: Study on pathways to improve the capacity for vertical collaboration of medical personnel in county-level medical alliances: an empirical exploration based on the CLFI collaboration model
items.abstract: To explore the key factors affecting the vertical collaboration of county and township medical personnel within county-level medical alliances and the paths for improvement, in order to provide suggestions for enhancing the intrinsic motivation for collaboration among county and township medical personnel. Based on D’Amour’s organizational collaboration theory, the CLFI vertical collaboration theoretical framework was constructed. Following this framework, a questionnaire was designed and administered using random sampling within one county-level medical alliance in Fujian Province, achieving a valid response rate of 96.95%. Ten dimensions, including shared goals and patient-centered orientation, were regarded as antecedent conditions. Fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis was employed to extract the pathways for enhancing the vertical collaboration capacity of county and township medical personnel. There are eight different configuration combinations, which can be summarized into five capability enhancement paths, namely the policy-driven path, the functional synergy path, the service-oriented path, the innovation-driven path, and the relationship-building path. The consistency of the solutions for these five combinations of causal conditions reached 82.2%. Strategically, policy coordination should be strengthened; cognitive linkages should be enhanced; patient outcomes should be embedded throughout the processes of collaborative goal setting, process design, and performance evaluation; a tolerance and assessment mechanism should be established to provide pilot support and dynamic monitoring for collaborative innovation; mutual trust among county and township medical personnel should be solidified, along with the consolidation of professional division of labor and capacity support, to promote the medical community’s transition from spontaneous cooperation to conscious coordination, ultimately achieving improved quality and efficiency in primary healthcare service capabilities. items.title: Sustained Engagement and Financial Readiness with AI-Based Learning Tools in Higher Education
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the teaching and working aspects in institutions of higher learning, but there is a lack of empirical knowledge on the economic preparedness and sustainability perception of the stakeholders. Most of the previous studies on educational technology adoption are based on behavioral intention and technological acceptance, though the economic sustainability (such as perceived economic value and affordability) is under-researched, especially in developing economies like India (Aaradhi and Chakraborty, 2024; Feng et al. , 2025). The research question of this paper is how the willingness to continue involvement with AI driven learning systems is determined by economic perceptions (value and affordability), financial access, and technological properties. Five universities in central India were sampled (412 students and faculty) and data were collected and then analyzed through Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). Findings indicate that perceived economic value and affordability affect the sustainability readiness in a positive way, and technological features enhance confidence in the long-term engagement. The results have a policy, university budgeting, and EdTech development strategies implication towards sustainable AI adoption.

items.title: Sycophantic AI, critical-feedback tolerance, and the case for productive friction in medical training
items.abstract: Concerns about generative AI in medical training often focus on eroded reasoning and deskilling. Such competence-based accounts are incomplete. We identify a neglected casualty: critical-feedback tolerance (CFT), the capacity to receive disconfirming evaluative feedback and remain productively engaged. Affirmation-optimized systems may lower CFT undetectably, surfacing only under authentic critique. This conceptual Perspective defines CFT, differentiates it from six established constructs, specifies measurable facets, and states explicit refutation conditions.

items.title: Synthesizing Geographical Semantics and Large Language Model for OD ‐Based Trajectory Captioning
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Trajectory captioning aims to represent trajectories in natural language texts, providing a human‐friendly approach to understanding and utilizing trajectory data. Previous trajectory captioning methods relied on manually defined rule templates to describe trajectories, failing to accurately and comprehensively capture the trajectory semantics. To address these issues, this paper synthesizes the semantics of the origin and destination (OD) points of trajectories with large language models (LLMs) to improve trajectory captioning. The proposed method first designs a trajectory context augmentation module that enriches the trajectories' context using the spatial information from Point‐of‐Interest (POI) distributions and human travel data from check‐in records. The method develops a geographical semantic‐based reasoning module that constructs a time‐subcategory graph and trains a POI matching module to capture the geographical semantics of the trajectories. Finally, a trajectory decoding module is developed, which leverages LLMs and the Chain‐of‐Thought inspired strategies to generate trajectory captions. Extensive experiments show that the proposed method outperforms baseline methods on both lexical‐overlap and semantic‐alignment metrics. This paper explores a new approach for trajectory semantics representation and provides a methodological reference for the text generation tasks in various geographical applications.

items.title: Targeted Protein Degradation: PROTACs, Molecular Glues, and the Future of Drug Discovery
items.abstract: The ability to selectively eliminate pathogenic proteins rather than merely inhibit their activity has redefined contemporary drug discovery, positioning targeted protein degradation (TPD) as one of the most significant advances in chemical biology and precision therapeutics.By harnessing endogenous protein quality-control machinery, TPD offers a catalytic and event-driven pharmacological strategy capable of addressing limitations associated with conventional occupancydriven inhibitors, including poor target selectivity, transient target engagement, acquired resistance, and the inaccessibility of many disease-relevant proteins.Among the expanding repertoire of degrader technologies, proteolysis-targeting chimeras (PROTACs) and molecular glues have emerged as the most mature and clinically advanced platforms, each employing distinct mechanisms to recruit E3 ubiquitin ligases and direct selective protein degradation.Their rapid evolution has been driven by breakthroughs in structural biology, medicinal chemistry, computational modeling, and artificial intelligence, enabling the rational design of degraders with enhanced potency, selectivity, and pharmacokinetic performance.Beyond oncology, these technologies are increasingly being explored for neurological, inflammatory, infectious, and rare genetic disorders, underscoring their broad therapeutic potential.Nevertheless, challenges related to E3 ligase diversity, tissue specificity, resistance mechanisms, safety, and clinical translation continue to influence their successful implementation.This review critically examines the molecular foundations, design principles, therapeutic applications, and clinical progress of PROTACs and molecular glues while integrating emerging targeted degradation platforms and technological innovations.Furthermore, it discusses the opportunities and unresolved challenges that will shape the next generation of degrader therapeutics and their transformative role in the future of precision drug discovery.

items.title: TD-interpreter: enhancing the understanding of timing diagrams with visual-language learning
items.abstract: Abstract We introduce TD-Interpreter, a specialised machine learning (ML) workflow that assists engineers in understanding complex timing diagrams (TDs), originating from a third party, during their design and verification process. The outcome of this workflow is a visual question-answer environment which allows engineers to input a set of TDs and ask design and verification queries regarding these TDs. To address limited training data availability, we developed a synthetic data generation pipeline that aligns visual information with its textual interpretation. We then implemented TD-Interpreter using a lightweight 7B Multimodal Large Language Model (MLLM), guided by both supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL). We also developed extensive TD-reasoning benchmarks from simple retrieval tasks to complex reasoning problems in the real world. Our experimental results show that TD-Interpreter substantially outperformed both the untuned base model, and commercial MLLMs (GPT-5.2), on the evaluated benchmarks, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed workflow.

items.title: TDD-Net: A Metadata-augmented Transformer Framework for Depression Detection from Primary Social Media Data
items.abstract: Mental illnesses are on the rise all over the world and there is a need to detect depression through digital footprints in an automated and early manner.The traditional Artificial Intelligence (AI) paradigms do not usually have context-based and user behavioral information.To overcome these shortcomings, this research paper suggested the Transformer-Based Depression Detection Network (TDD-Net) that combined textual information with user-centric behavioral metadata built on a fully primary and consented social media dataset.The data included self-written posts, captions, comments, patterns of interactions and anonymized profile data.Text cleaning, sentiment normalization and tokenization were done by using a systematic preprocessing pipeline.A RoBERTa encoder was used to learn the semantic representation of text, and a metadata embedding network was used to learn longitudinal behavioral signals, including posting frequency, intensity of engagement, and diurnal activity patterns.The linguistic and metadata vectors were fused with a fusion layer and a multi-head attention classification head was applied to predict the risk of depression.This transformer fusion, which is metadata-enhanced, boosted personalization in depression detection.An experimental assessment revealed an accuracy of 97.18, and better precision, recall, and F1-scores.These findings show that the model has high predictive accuracy, and it is used in practice in mental health monitoring.TDD-Net is a big improvement over the conventional text-only approach by making good use of extensive behavioral cues.

items.title: Teacher-guided Pseudo-supervised Dance Human Video Segmentation via Open-vocabulary Localization and SAM2 Masklet Propagation
items.abstract: Dance videos combine rapid non-rigid motion, limb crossings, deformable costumes, and changing illumination, which make human segmentation vulnerable to boundary loss, identity switches, and temporal flicker.We present DanceMask-SAM, a teacher-guided pseudo-supervised framework that constructs dance pseudo supervision without frame-wise masks from target training videos.Offline, open-vocabulary localization provides global-human and local-structure prompts, and overlapping bidirectional SAM2 masklets provide redundant candidates.Prompt credibility, dance-aware reliability, and disagreement arbitration assign candidates to hard supervision, weak consistency, or rejection.Online, a fixed MobileNetV3-Large-FPN student uses single RGB frames only and therefore requires no text prompt, SAM2, or pose estimator at deployment.On the manually reviewed test protocol, the complete student obtains 0.872 mIoU, 0.875 J&F, and 0.061 MFR; across three seeds, the corresponding means are 0.874, 0.877, and 0.061.The final student is close to, but does not exceed, the teacher-fused pseudo-label quality reported for reliability plus arbitration (0.874 mIoU and 0.876 J&F).Video-level, Bonferroni-corrected tests support the reported comparisons within the stated split.External validation on Zhuang ethnic dance videos yields 0.824 J&F, confirming transfer under domain shift.Threshold-frozen protocol details, baseline interaction budgets, reliability sensitivity, risk-coverage bands with video-level confidence intervals, teacher compute cost and failure boundaries are reported in Section IV.The contribution is limited to pseudo-supervision construction and training decisions under teacher-guided pseudo-labels, rather than a new foundation model, a new student architecture, or a self-supervised representation-learning result.

items.title: Teaching and psychological associations of adolescent piano composition skills: a study on constructivist practices and reflective guidance based on teacher reports
items.abstract: Introduction To understand the connection between open teaching environments and musical creative performance, this study focuses on adolescent piano teaching, examining the structural associations among constructivist practices, reflective guidance, and piano composition skills, and analyzing the parallel indirect associations linked via creative self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation for composition. Methods A cross-sectional questionnaire design was adopted, based on the analysis of 723 self-reports from teachers with adolescent piano teaching experience and their evaluation data on students’ states and skills. Multivariate regression and Bootstrap resampling methods were used for statistical path testing, comparing group distribution characteristics under different learning purposes, and testing the boundary conditions formed by the frequency of composition teaching. Results (1) Both constructivist practices and reflective guidance showed significant positive associations with the evaluated piano composition skills; (2) Creative self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation for composition presented significant parallel indirect paths in the above associations; (3) The overall differences among groups with different learning purposes on all core constructs reached statistical significance, with the descriptive means of the grading test or competition group generally being lower than those of the hobby group; (4) No significant moderating phenomenon of composition teaching frequency on the association between constructivist practices and intrinsic motivation was found. Discussion Autonomous decision-making and process scrutiny are independently and positively associated with teacher-evaluated student composition skills, respectively. These teaching practice characteristics, together with students’ capability beliefs and internal willingness to participate, constitute the relevant conditions for musical practice. However, as these internal psychological states are inferred by teachers for whole groups rather than evaluated at the individual level, interpretations regarding direct psychological mechanisms remain limited. In teaching applications, compared with simply increasing the frequency of activities, improving the design quality of open and reflective tasks may be of more practical significance.

items.title: Teaching with AI, Not Against It: A Thinking Partner Framework for Working Adult Learners in Compressed Online Formats
items.abstract: Working adult learners in online graduate programs face challenges that make strict AI bans both impractical and unhelpful. This paper introduces the Thinking Partner Framework, a practical approach to AI integration developed and refined across six semesters of graduate research methods courses serving approximately 440 K-12 educators. Instead of treating AI as a problem to be detected, the framework positions AI as a Socratic partner that helps students learn while still requiring them to think for themselves. Five design principles—transparency, process documentation, authentic assessment, scaffolded autonomy, and metacognitive reflection—guide the framework’s implementation. The paper includes practical tools such as sample prompts, documentation templates, and examples illustrating the difference between using AI for answers and using it as a thinking partner. Observations from practice, including a 96% checkpoint completion rate and evidence of students transferring Socratic techniques to their own classrooms, suggest promise, though more rigorous research is needed. This framework gives distance education administrators a practical option beyond simply banning or allowing AI. Keywords: artificial intelligence, adult learning, distance education, Socratic method, academic integrity, compressed courses

items.title: Technostress in the age of digital transformation and AI: A bibliometric–systematic literature review for HRM research
items.abstract: Digital transformation and artificial intelligence are reshaping human resource management through algorithmic recruitment, automated evaluation, predictive analytics, and generative tools. While these systems improve efficiency, they also intensify technostress through opacity, surveillance, reduced control, and digitally intensified work arrangements. Responding to a fragmented literature spanning both AI-enabled and broader digital work systems, this study provides a B-SLR that maps technostress in digital transformation while identifying AI-specific stressors as a key emerging stream for HRM research. Drawing on 194 Scopus-indexed articles, we combine performance analysis and science mapping to identify publication trends, dominant themes, and intellectual structures. The review shows how AI-specific stressors extend established technostress mechanisms and shift attention toward transparency, control, fairness, and responsible HRM design. We conclude with actionable implications for researchers and practitioners aiming to design more transparent, responsible, and sustainable digital and AI-enabled HRM systems.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: The adoption, efficacy, and limitations of large language models in urological education
items.abstract: The integration of large language models into medical education is rapidly transforming pedagogical approaches, particularly in specialized fields like urology. This study aims to evaluate the adoption patterns, perceived efficacy, and significant limitations of these artificial intelligence (AI) tools among urology trainees. This research employed a descriptive, cross-sectional study design through an online survey disseminated to urology trainees at a single institution. A total of 194 complete responses were collected from medical students and interns. The survey assessed adoption patterns, perceived efficacy on a 7-point Likert-scale, and limitations. The analysis revealed near-universal adoption (98.4%), with 65% of participants using AI tools daily, predominantly ChatGPT. Key applications included generating exam-style questions and summarizing complex guidelines. Participants reported significant perceived improvements in core knowledge areas, with the highest gains in disease knowledge and diagnostics (Median = 7, interquartile range: 6–7), which were strongly correlated with increased clinical confidence. Multivariate regression identified usage frequency and comfort with technology as significant predictors of knowledge improvement (β = 0.29, P = .001) and confidence gains (β = 0.30, P < .001). The primary limitation identified was the potential for AI “hallucinations” or incorrect information (54.1%). Large language models are widely adopted and perceived as highly effective for enhancing knowledge and clinical reasoning in urological education. However, their transformative potential is tempered by critical concerns regarding reliability. A balanced approach that combines these powerful AI tools with vigilant oversight is essential.

items.title: The AI Trust Gap: Consumer Perceptions of AI-Powered Digital Marketing
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in digital marketing to personalize communications, recommend products, and automate customer interactions. Despite these capabilities, consumer trust in AI-powered marketing remains uncertain. This exploratory study examines consumer perceptions of AI-driven digital marketing using survey data collected from 500 U.S. adults. Findings suggest that consumers generally recognize the usefulness of AI-powered marketing but remain cautious about whether organizations using AI act in consumers’ best interests. Respondents expressed concerns regarding privacy, data use, and organizational trustworthiness, while transparency and data security emerged as important trust-building factors. Moderate daily AI users (2–5 hours) reported higher levels of trust in companies employing AI-driven marketing practices than light users (<2 hours). Overall, the findings suggest that consumer acceptance of AI’s functional benefits does not necessarily translate into trust in organizations that deploy these technologies. Implications for marketing managers and directions for future research are discussed.

items.title: The AI-augmented researcher: Optimizing systematic reviews in ergonomics
items.abstract: BackgroundThe emergence of Academic Artificial Intelligence (AAI) agents is reshaping Systematic Literature Reviews (SLR) by expanding evidence screening and synthesis beyond Boolean, metadata-based searches, but its use requires a clear, PRISMA-aligned human oversight model to avoid compromising research integrity.ObjectiveThis opinion article proposes the "AI-augmented researcher" as a multidimensional framework that synergizes human analytical rigor with Large Language Models (LLMs). Using a physical ergonomics case study, the paper establishes a normative integration strategy that demonstrates how AAI can accelerate evidence synthesis while maintaining strict PRISMA compliance under explicit human oversight.MethodologyA Workflow Comparative Analysis (WCA) applying a parallel-group design to physical ergonomics SLR. The procedure synchronized two approaches: 1) A "classical" SLR workflow, using Boolean syntax and paratextual screening (Metadata) across indexed databases; and 2) An AAI-driven workflow, utilizing LLM-based immersion via natural language prompting. Comparative metrics analyzed included execution time, record processing volume, and the identification of emerging trends-such as Ergonomics 4.0-benchmarked against the PRISMA 2020 protocol.ResultsThe AAI-augmented workflow reduced execution time by 96% (39 h to 1.5 h) while increasing record processing by 370%. Qualitatively, iterative prompting fostered a "hermeneutic dialogue," enabling the detection of complex "Ergonomics 4.0" trends obscured in syntactic searches.ConclusionsAAI serves as a cognitive enhancer, reconfiguring the researcher from a "data miner" to an "evidence curator". While efficiency is optimized, strict human oversight remains indispensable to mitigate algorithmic hallucinations and ensure ethical scientific integrity.

items.title: The Cognitive Cost of LLM Writing: A Reading-Time Comparison with Human Text
items.abstract: Although linguistic differences between human-written and Large Language Model (LLM)-generated texts have been extensively studied, their implications for the cognitive effort involved in reading remain less explored. In psycholinguistics, reading time is commonly used as an indirect measure of cognitive processing effort. Building on this perspective, we investigate whether human-written texts and their LLM-generated rewrites exhibit differences in predicted reading time that may reflect differences in processing demands for readers. To this end, we introduce RoBERTa-RT, a model trained on human eye-tracking data to predict word-level reading times. We evaluate the model on both internal and external test sets, construct a paired dataset of 496 human-written articles and their LLM-generated rewrites, and apply RoBERTa-RT to compare their predicted reading times. Our findings show that LLM-generated rewrites tend to be shorter and have slightly lower predicted total reading times, while exhibiting higher predicted reading times per word. These differences are associated with systematic linguistic changes, including longer and less frequent words, greater lexical diversity, and higher contextual predictability. From a cognitive perspective, our findings suggest that LLM-generated writing may redistribute reading demands: reducing the amount of text to process while increasing the predicted processing effort associated with individual words. This highlights the importance of considering not only the linguistic characteristics of machine-generated content, but also its potential implications for human cognitive processing.

items.title: THE CRITICAL EQUATION: OCCUPATIONAL STRESSORS AND THEIR CONSEQUENTIAL CORROSION OF PEDAGOGICAL EFFICIENCY IN HIGHER EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS OF KANNYAKUMARI DISTRICT
items.abstract: Occupational burnout serves as a structural roadblock for educators within higher education, directly eroding classroom performance, institutional morale, and pedagogical delivery. This empirical inquiry maps the precise structural catalysts of workplace anxiety, its downstream impacts on classroom effectiveness, and the adaptive behaviors utilized by educators across the Arts and Science colleges of Kanyakumari District. Relying on a quantitative methodology, data was extracted from 235 faculty members through proportionate random sampling. The empirical findings indicate that hyper-extended work hours, administrative bloat, crushing deadlines, and systemic institutional isolation act as primary institutional stressors. Elevated stress significantly undermines instructional vitality, diminishes intrinsic motivation, and reduces academic performance. Conversely, teachers backed by structural wellness infrastructure and professional counseling frameworks displayed notably better teaching outcomes. The study advocates for structural workload limits, institutional wellness mandates, and systemic career development pathways to preserve academic excellence.

items.title: The Declarative Delegation Method: A Governance Framework for Transparent AI-Assisted Scholarship
items.abstract: Scholars and professionals now routinely produce papers, presentations, and reports with generative AI, yet may disclose that work in a single footnote: "AI was used." That footnote is true and uninformative. It does not say who conceived the argument, who wrote the prose, who checked the claims, or who answers for them. This paper proposes the Declarative Delegation Method, a declared, citable methodology for AI-assisted knowledge work. It does not invent human-governed AI-assisted scholarship, which many experienced researchers already practice; it converts that diffuse practice into an explicit, citable governance methodology with defined decision rights and verification gates. A human principal treats AI systems as an unlimited-budget team of advisors and contractors, retains every judgment-bearing decision, and delegates drafting, elaboration, and review under explicit role constraints and verification gates. The method is an applied instance of the delegation relationship developed across the author's twelve-paper canon: judgment-bounded delegation (C05), delegation quality and escalation (C04), persona as a delegation constraint (C08), governance as architecture (C09), and the evaluability condition (C11). Its central claim extends that last paper's evaluability condition: the integrity of an AI-assisted work's production process can be audited only if the process that produced it was declared in advance. The paper specifies the method's roles, decision rights, workflow, and disclosure standard; positions it within the authorship debate through the senior-author analogy; states its strengths, limits, and scope, including where it must not be used; and sets out how it can be tested with publicly available data. Individual works can then cite the method and report a per-work disclosure profile instead of a footnote. The method is offered as a proposed standard, not yet a validated one; its dependence on expert principals, on self-attestation and on institutional incentives is stated as a limit, not resolved.Revision 1 corrects the wording of the disclosure section and standard statements so that the author, not the AI system, is the agent of every action. The method is unchanged (v1.0).

items.title: The double-edged sword of human-AI collaboration on design students’ competence development: The mediating roles of challenge and hindrance appraisals and the asymmetric moderation of teacher AI leadership
items.abstract: The deepening integration of generative AI into design education is driving a paradigm shift in human-computer AI collaboration (HAIC) -from mere tool assistance toward intelligent synergy. However, its dual impact on the competency development of design students and the underlying mechanisms remain insufficiently understood. Grounded in the Theory of Stress Appraisal, this study constructs a research model to examine the double-edged sword effect of HAIC on Design Competence (DC), introducing teacher AI Leadership (AIL) as a moderating variable. The aim is to reveal the psychological mechanisms and boundary conditions through which HAIC influences DC. Employing a questionnaire survey, this study conducted an empirical investigation involving 483 design students in East China. Data analysis was performed using SPSS 24.0 and Amos 23.0, encompassing reliability and validity tests, regression analysis, and Bootstrap mediation analysis. The results indicate that HAIC influences DC through dual pathways: it positively enhances DC by fostering Challenge Appraisal (CA) (β = 0.283, p < 0.01), which in turn positively predicted competence development (β = 0.363, p < 0.01), yielding a significant indirect effect of 0.103 (p < 0.01). Simultaneously, HAIC triggered Hindrance Appraisal (HA) (β = 0.271, p < 0.01), which negatively predicted competence development (β = −0.229, p < 0.01), yielding a significant indirect effect of −0.062 (p < 0.01). This constitutes a partial mediating mechanism characterized by “one positive, one negative” effect. Furthermore, Teacher AIL exhibits an asymmetric moderating effect: it significantly buffers the positive impact of HAIC on HA (β = −0.112, p < 0.01), indicating that high AIL can mitigate cognitive load and anxiety arising from technological uncertainty, yet it does not significantly amplify the positive pathway via CA (β = 0.001, p > 0.05). The findings suggest that the impact of HAIC on DC is not linear but rather a dialectical process contingent upon individual cognitive appraisal. The core value of Teacher AIL lies in “risk mitigation” rather than “creativity stimulation,” offering a theoretical foundation for the intelligent transformation of educational design. At the practical level, it is imperative to facilitate from knowledge deliverers to cognitive facilitators in AI-augmented design education. By systematically developing AI instructional competencies and reforming assessment systems, educators can guide students toward establishing a healthy relationship with HAIC, thereby achieving the synergistic advancement of technological empowerment and humanistic literacy.

items.title: The Ethics of Prompt Engineering
items.abstract: Prompt engineering is commonly understood as a technical practice aimed at eliciting useful, accurate, and appropriately structured outputs from large language models (LLMs). Yet prompts do more than optimize model performance: they shape what information is elicited, which assumptions are introduced, and which perspectives are privileged. In this paper, we argue that prompting should therefore be understood as an epistemic and normative act. We distinguish between two conceptions of prompting: knowledge generation, in which the model is implicitly treated as an epistemic authority, and knowledge injection, in which users provide relevant knowledge, evidence, and context that the model can organize, articulate, and extend. We contend that the latter provides a more appropriate model for responsible LLM use, since prompting cannot substitute for subject-matter expertise or the critical evaluation of model outputs. At the same time, prompts inevitably inject values, intentions, and assumptions into the generation process. Building on these premises, we propose five principles for responsible prompting: epistemic humility, explicit engagement with uncertainty and epistemic underdetermination, source sensitivity, avoidance of deceptive framing, and recognition of model limitations and appropriate task allocation. We further argue that responsibility for AI-generated outputs is distributed across users, developers, institutions, and societies, and that some applications cannot be rendered ethical through better prompting alone.

items.title: The Illusion of Security
items.abstract: This chapter critically examines the assumption that artificial intelligence (AI)-powered cybersecurity inherently strengthens data protection within educational environments. Drawing on a critical review of interdisciplinary literature, it argues that the rapid adoption of AI-driven educational technologies has outpaced the development of effective governance, resulting in significant challenges relating to data privacy, transparency, provenance, informed consent, human-centered design, and cybersecurity. Rather than viewing these issues as isolated concerns, the chapter demonstrates how they interact to create an illusion of security, whereby systems marketed as protective may simultaneously introduce new vulnerabilities and accountability gaps. It concludes that addressing these challenges requires an integrated approach that combines cybersecurity, human-computer interaction, AI governance, and educational policy to develop more transparent, ethical, and user-centered AI-mediated learning environments.

items.abstract: The infusion of Artificial Intelligence technologies, particularly conversational marketing, has become a vital contributor to the digital transformation. This transformation has significantly reshaped customer interactions within the banking sector. The study aims to investigate how the deployment of conversational marketing impacts digital overhaul and customer interaction in the Indian banking sector. This research employed is exploratory approach with a structured questionnaire to collect data using purposive sampling. The research information was primarily gathered by collecting primary data from 100 respondents in Indore, India, and statistical tools like Exploratory Factor Analysis (EFA) and regression analysis with R 2 is 0.77 were employed to analyze the data. The findings revealed that the adoption of tools of conversational marketing significantly influences online customer interaction, which plays a crucial role in digital transformation. The limitation of this study is limited participant base and it&s;s restricted to only Indore district. The study highlights the importance of conversational marketing for Indian banks, which improves customer interaction and service efficiency by automating repetitive operations, delivering 24/7 support, and creating a customized experience. This offers valuable insight for the Indian banking sector to promote in a rapidly changing digital world.

items.title: The Impact of Generative AI on the Future of Work: Opportunities, Risks, and Human Skills
items.abstract: Background: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has expanded the range of cognitive tasks that can be assisted by software, raising questions about productivity, job displacement, and the future value of human skills. Objective: To critically synthesize selected empirical and institutional evidence concerning productivity, occupational exposure, adoption, and skill complementarity. Methods: This narrative review draws on a purposively selected set of peer-reviewed studies, working papers, and institutional reports published primarily between 2023 and 2026. It does not claim systematic coverage or PRISMA-ScR compliance. Findings: Controlled experiments document substantial productivity gains for some writing and programming tasks, while workplace evidence suggests heterogeneity across experience levels. Occupational exposure estimates indicate the scope for task transformation but do not measure realized job losses. Adoption studies show that workplace use is growing, yet aggregate outcomes remain uncertain. Creative assistance may raise individual performance while narrowing output diversity. Conclusions: The future of work is better understood through task reallocation, complementary skills, organizational implementation, and distributional choices than through simple predictions of mass replacement. Further longitudinal and cross-country research is needed. Keywords: generative artificial intelligence; future of work; productivity; employment; occupational exposure; human skills; narrative review

items.title: The influence of AI adoption on decision making, forecasting, and performance: Evidence from solar and telecommunication sectors in Pakistan and China
items.abstract: This study investigates how Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption builds sustainable supply chain performance in the renewable energy and telecommunications sectors, focusing on the mediating mechanisms of decision-making and forecasting. Using a comparative design, data was collected from 214 companies in Pakistan and China. The proposed model was analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), integrating the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework and Resource-Based View (RBV). Results confirm a fully mediated pathway, AI adoption is positively associated with decision making and forecasting capabilities, which are positively associated with operational and financial performance, and are associated stronger supply chain performance. A key finding is that these capabilities exert no direct effect, revealing that AI's sustainability impact is realized indirectly through core business outcomes. The comparative analysis highlights contextual influence, with China's mature ecosystem fostering deep AI integration and Pakistan's emerging context showing reliance on external tools. This study provides a novel, integrated TOE-RBV model that unpacks the "black box" of AI's impact on sustainability. It offers unique empirical evidence from contrasting emerging economies, demonstrating that the path to AI-driven sustainable supply chains is mediated and context-dependent. For managers, embedding AI into core processes is critical for sustainability gains. For policymakers, strategies must be context-specific, focusing on foundational digital infrastructure in emerging economies and advanced innovation ecosystems in mature ones.

items.title: The Lunar Human Environment
items.abstract: Chapter 9 The lunar environment is an extreme and hostile, the absence of atmosphere means it has wide temperature swings, intense radiation exposure, and complete silence. The Moon’s surface is covered in fine, electrostatically charged dust (regolith), which clings to equipment and poses both operational and health risks. Astronauts describe this surface as powdery yet uneven, with occasional hard areas, and movement is affected by the Moon’s one‑sixth gravity. Without atmospheric or magnetic protection, the Moon is exposed to solar and cosmic radiation, making shielding essential for human survival. For people to live and work carefully engineered microclimates, such as spacesuits and pressurised habitats will be required. Environmental ergonomics principles still apply but must be adapted, as behavioural adjustments are limited and replaced by tightly controlled systems. Sustainable lunar living depends on closed loop life support systems that manage air, water, food, waste, and energy. Habitat design is central, focusing on radiation shielding, thermal control, energy efficiency, and self-sufficiency for long-term human habitation on the Moon.

items.title: The Mediating Role of Adaptive Strategies in the Relationship between Work-Related Challenges and Teaching Effectiveness and Job Satisfaction of TVL (Technical -Vocational-Livelihood) Teachers: A Basis for a Professional Development Program
items.abstract: This study examined the mediating role of adaptive strategies in the relationship between work-related challenges and teaching effectiveness and job satisfaction among Technical-Vocational-Livelihood (TVL) teachers as a basis for developing a professional development program. Anchored in the Job Demands–Resources Model, Transactional Theory of Stress and Coping, and Herzberg’s Two-Factor Theory, the study employed a quantitative descriptive-correlational research design with mediation analysis. Using universal sampling, 40 TVL teachers from five public secondary schools in Bilar, Batuan, and Carmen, Bohol, participated in the study. Data were collected through a modified and expert-validated questionnaire using a four-point Likert scale and analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and regression-based mediation analysis at a 0.05 significance level. Results revealed high levels of work-related challenges (M = 3.05), adaptive strategies (M = 3.43), and teaching effectiveness (M = 3.56), while job satisfaction was moderate (M = 3.17). Student-related concerns and resource adequacy emerged as the major challenges, whereas technology and artificial intelligence-assisted teaching received the highest adaptive strategy rating. Work-related challenges showed no statistically significant relationships with adaptive strategies, teaching effectiveness, or job satisfaction. Adaptive strategies were significantly associated with teaching effectiveness (r = .392, p = .012) but not with job satisfaction (r = .003, p = .986). Moreover, no significant mediating effects were established for either professional outcome. The findings informed the proposed Adaptive and Industry-Responsive Professional Development Program, emphasizing instructional innovation, professional collaboration, institutional support, and teacher well-being. The study aligns with Sustainable Development Goals 3 (Good Health and Well-Being), 4 (Quality Education), and 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth). Its potential sustainability contribution lies in strengthening educational quality, institutional responsiveness, teacher welfare, and industry-relevant workforce preparation through evidence-based professional development.

items.title: The Mediterranean Diet as a Pillar of Sustainable and Humanistic Education
items.abstract: The Mediterranean Diet (MD) is a foundational cornerstone for addressing global sustainability crises and contemporary educational imperatives. Recognised as an alternative to unsustainable food structures, this lifestyle integrates nutritional value, environmental conservation, and cultural heritage. Despite these benefits, regional populations have increasingly abandoned this pattern, generating socio-ecological and public health complications. To counter this regression, this chapter evaluates how the MD directly advances the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Furthermore, the authors illustrate how transitioning from a clinical interpretation of nutrition toward a humanistic educational model fosters environmental empathy. Specifically, this chapter examines the practical integration of inclusive pedagogical frameworks, such as Universal Design for Learning, alongside digital interventions like Augmented Reality (AR) and Artificial Intelligence (AI), redefining the classroom as a living laboratory for democratic citizenship and nutritional equity.

items.title: The Missing Interface: Why Complex Projects Fail Where Nobody Is Looking
items.abstract: Complex projects are assumed to be coordinated when their documents are aligned. This article argues that the assumption fails in a specific and costly way. Projects often fail at their human interfaces, the boundaries between people, teams and organisations where shared understanding either exists or does not, while the management systems mainly measure the technical and documentary layer. Drawing on publicly documented cases, including the opening of Heathrow Terminal 5, the Mars Climate Orbiter and Ariane 5 flight 501, the article names this gap the Illusion of Coordination and proposes Human Interface Management (HIM) as the missing counterpart to Technical Interface Management (TIM). It introduces N² + H, a model that adds human layers to the N² matrix of systems engineering: beneath each cell of the matrix sit the owners on each side and the state of the relationship between them, a property called Interface Depth. It also introduces Interface Health, an assessment of five human factors: clarity of responsibility, communication quality, decision speed, trust and delivery capability. The two disciplines together are called Integrated Interface Management (IIM), which the article places in the sociotechnical systems tradition. This is the first public article in a larger body of work.

items.title: The Next Generation of Crime Solvers
items.abstract: Chapter 21 examines the rise of artificial intelligence, machine learning, and predictive analytics in modern policing. It explores how algorithms analyze crime patterns, forecast hot spots, and support resource allocation. Readers learn how AI enhances forensic analysis, automates data processing, and identifies digital anomalies. The chapter also addresses ethical concerns, including algorithmic bias, transparency, civil liberties, and the risk of overreliance on automated systems. The case study illustrate both the promise and pitfalls of predictive policing. Ultimately, Chapter 21 argues that AI must be used responsibly, with strong oversight, to ensure fairness and effectiveness in future crime analysis. This discussion underscores the need for continuous evaluation of algorithmic tools to ensure they align with evolving legal standards and societal expectations.

items.title: The Non-Technical User as an LLM Threat Vector: Linguistic Strategies for Bypassing AI Safeguards and Implications for AI Security
items.abstract: The threat that ordinary non-technical users pose to large language models (LLMs) still sits at the margins of AI-security research. These are people who work with AI assistants every day — at work, in study, in everyday life — yet hold no specialised background in information technology or machine learning. A post-laboratory survey of first-year humanities undergraduates (n=70) returned an unexpectedly high figure: 95.7% cleared all main protection levels of the Gandalf platform (Lakera AI) without stepping outside purely linguistic techniques. These included sign-form decomposition and formatting (M=2.00), cross-language code-switching (M=1.29), indirect semantic extraction (20.3% of open-ended responses), and pragmatic pressure. We read these micro-level data against the macro picture of the Gandalf-RCT crowdsourcing experiment (279,675 prompts) and against academic work on filter evasion in image-generation systems (SurrogatePrompt, PC², DALL-E 3, Shedevrum/Yandex). The pattern runs through all of them. From text LLMs to multimodal generators, the filter yields to the same moves, none of which require a line of code: a proper name is swapped for a physical description, direct reference for allegory or an adjacent associative term, the prompt language is switched, the grapheme is distorted. A three-tier analysis of LLM break-resistance grounds the paper’s central claim — that rising everyday AI literacy produces a structural security deficit left uncovered by current surface-level filtering. Several implications for AI safety system design follow.

items.title: THE PEDAGOGICAL SIGNIFICANCE OF ORGANIZING INTERACTIVE LESSONS BASED ON DIGITAL TECHNOLOGIES
items.abstract: This article investigates the pedagogical significance of digitally supported interactive lessons and proposes a research-informed approach to their planning and evaluation. Rather than equating interactivity with screen use or frequent clicking, it conceptualizes interactive teaching as purposeful engagement in questioning, explanation, problem solving, collaboration, feedback, and reflection. The analysis integrates constructive alignment, the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework, the ICAP model of cognitive engagement, formative assessment principles, and inclusive learning design. A six-stage instructional cycle is proposed: activation, inquiry, collaborative construction, application, formative feedback, and reflection. An illustrative 60-minute teacher-education lesson shows how digital tools can support the stages while retaining essential face-to-face dialogue. A comparative matrix identifies relationships among instructional technologies, student actions, and assessment evidence. The discussion addresses learner agency, cognitive overload, digital inequality, accessibility, data protection, and the responsible use of artificial intelligence. The contribution is conceptual and methodological; it offers operational criteria for lesson quality and directions for future classroom evaluation, but it does not claim experimentally verified improvements. The central conclusion is that digital interactivity has pedagogical value only when it produces observable, cognitively meaningful learner activity.

items.title: The Perceived Benefits and Challenges of fertility Awareness Based Methods of Contraception: A scoping review
items.abstract: Background: Fertility Awareness-Based Methods (FABMs) are increasingly recognised for their potential to support reproductive autonomy, inclusivity across cultural, religious, and ethical contexts, and freedom from pharmacological side effects. However, their uptake and sustained use remain uneven, shaped by knowledge requirements, training demands, relational dynamics, and limited integration into mainstream healthcare systems. Methods: A scoping review was conducted to map empirical evidence on perceived benefits and challenges of FABMs. Studies published between 2012 and 2025 were identified across global settings. Eligible studies employed qualitative, quantitative, or mixed-methods designs and focused on user-reported perceptions of FABMs. Studies involving refugees or asylum seekers were excluded. Data extraction was supported by chatGPT and subsequently verified manually prior to thematic analysis. Results: Findings revealed distinct themes categorised into perceived benefits and challenges. Reported benefits included the non-hormonal nature of FABMs, avoidance of pharmacological side effects, enhanced emotional well-being, increased reproductive literacy, and a sense of autonomy and trust arising from greater understanding of menstrual cycles and bodily patterns. Despite these benefits, practical and methodological challenges emerged as the most frequently reported barriers, including difficulties identifying fertility biomarkers, charting accuracy, daily monitoring demands, and variability in instructional quality. These challenges suggest underlying gaps in reproductive health knowledge and access to trained providers. Less commonly reported barriers related to relational dynamics, including abstinence-related tension, concerns about reliability in the absence of structured support, and context-specific intimacy strain. Conclusions: While FABMs offer perceived benefits related to autonomy, trust, and well-being, their effective adoption depends on robust education, consistent instructional quality, and supportive relational and healthcare contexts. Interventions such as clinician training using digital decision-support tools, alongside peer mentoring and targeted user education, may help address identified barriers. Findings should be interpreted cautiously, given the scope of included studies. Future research should evaluate how educational and clinical interventions influence acceptability, sustained use, and health outcomes over time.

items.title: The power of AI: balancing ethics and harm for the environmental justice field
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence, after the boom of generative AI, is beginning to shape environmental decision-making, at the same moment that environmental justice (EJ) communities face intensifying ecological harm, federal disinvestment, and data erasure. This paper examines the dual tensions AI presents for the EJ field: its potential as a tool for democratizing data access and amplifying community knowledge, and its reproduction of the very hierarchies EJ seeks to dismantle. We document harms across several domains, including the environmental racism embedded in data center siting and energy demand, the extension of fossil fuel industry lifespans, data bias and digital colonialism in AI training, access and literacy inequities, data privacy risks, technological hallucination, and technological solutionism. Drawing on thirty years of community-centered data practice at an EJ nonprofit, we propose an alternative paradigm grounded in the Community Advisory Board model, data democratization, community co-creation, and ethical data governance. This includes community-governed data trusts, accessible data infrastructure, and AI tools designed to build rather than replace community capacity. EJ communities must not only hold AI accountable for its harms but also ask the question of how the technology’s capabilities can serve justice rather than just capital interest.

items.title: The Privacy-Personalization Paradox in AI-Driven Customer Experience Analytics: A Trust-Centred Integrative Review and Responsible Personalization Framework
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly supports personalised customer experiences through predictive analytics, recommender systems, behavioural profiling and conversational interfaces. However, the data collection and inference required for personalisation can also heighten perceptions of surveillance, vulnerability and loss of control. This integrative conceptual review examines how AI-enabled personalisation, perceived privacy risk and consumer trust interact within customer experience analytics. The synthesis integrates privacy calculus, social exchange, psychological reactance and signalling perspectives to explain how consumers evaluate personalisation value against privacy-related costs. A trust-centred framework is developed in which personalisation intensity, data sensitivity, algorithmic inference and recommendation relevance jointly shape perceived value and privacy risk, with consumer trust linking these evaluations to engagement, disclosure willingness, satisfaction, loyalty and continued use. The review also distinguishes actual data practices from perceived privacy intrusion and identifies contextual conditions that may alter this balance. The review further proposes a context-dependent nonlinear relationship between personalisation intensity and trust: moderate personalisation may strengthen trust when relevance and value are proportionate to data use, whereas more intensive personalisation may reduce trust when intrusion, surveillance or loss of autonomy becomes salient. Responsible personalisation is therefore framed around proportionate data use, meaningful transparency, consumer control and privacy-by-design. The framework and proposed personalisation threshold remain conceptual and require empirical testing across AI applications, cultural settings and regulatory environments.

items.title: The Reliance Hypothesis: Chain-of-Thought Faithfulness Rises as Language Resource Level Falls
items.abstract: Chain-of-Thought (CoT) faithfulness matters for monitoring, explaining and safely deploying large language models, yet it has been studied mostly in English. Languages differ in level, the amount of text available to learn from, so models know less in lower-resource languages, which may change how much they rely on their reasoning. To our knowledge, we are the first to relate CoT faithfulness to both resource level and task type (knowledge- or reasoning-intensive). On parallel multiple-choice questions from Multilingual Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMMLU) in eight languages, faithfulness rises as resource level falls on knowledge-intensive tasks but not on reasoning-intensive ones, a gap that points the same way across four models and several faithfulness measures. We propose, and find support for, the Reliance Hypothesis: models rely more on their reasoning when they cannot recall the answer, as in lower-resource languages on knowledge-intensive tasks. Model confidence partly explains the effect of resource level, but not the knowledge-reasoning gap. Languages in which models are less confident rely more on reasoning, yet less confident answers within a language do not, a Simpson's paradox. In lower-resource languages, models rely on their reasoning for more answers, not more strongly for each. CoT monitoring may therefore be most informative in lower-resource languages, where it is least often validated.

items.title: The role of artificial intelligence in business model innovation: an integrative framework and research agenda
items.abstract: Purpose Given the rapid introduction of new technologies into organizational environments, there is currently a need to understand which economic, technological and social factors can influence organizations to implement artificial intelligence (AI) in order to stimulate innovation. Thus, this research seeks to understand how the literature on the influence of AI on business model innovation has evolved, discovering which factors drive organizational interest on the part of organizations and how they can benefit with its implementation. Design/methodology/approach To this end, a bibliometric methodology was employed, complemented by an in-depth analytical review of each article. The analysis covered the period from the emergence of the research field to 2026, resulting in the systematic examination of 117 studies published within this timeframe. Findings Based on the bibliometric analysis, the articles were grouped into three clusters representing the main research streams in the field. The findings show that AI-driven business model innovation relies on dynamic capabilities, organizational resilience, strategic alignment, governance mechanisms and human–AI complementarity. The study also provides strategic insights to help organizations align AI adoption with their specific characteristics and contexts. Originality/value After creating an individual framework for each cluster, an integrative vision of AI in business model innovation was created, bringing together all the concepts under study, as well as an agenda for future research.

items.title: The Role of Emerging Technologies in Shaping Modern Banking and Financial Services
items.abstract: Emerging technologies are significantly transforming the landscape of banking and financial services, shifting the way institutions operate and how consumers engage with financial products. Technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI), blockchain, big data analytics, and cloud computing have moved beyond theoretical concepts and are now at the core of innovation within the financial sector. These tools are streamlining operations, enhancing customer service, improving security, and enabling the development of more inclusive and user-centric financial services. This paper explores how these technologies are making banking systems faster, smarter, more efficient, and accessible to a broader population. AI is being used for fraud detection, predictive analytics, and virtual customer assistance. Blockchain is enabling secure, decentralized financial transactions with increased transparency. Big data is helping institutions understand customer behavior and tailor services accordingly, while cloud computing allows for more agile and scalable infrastructure, enabling banks to respond more quickly to market changes. While the benefits of these advancements are substantial, they also come with a new set of challenges. Issues such as cybersecurity vulnerabilities, regulatory compliance, data privacy, and digital inclusion must be carefully addressed to ensure that technological progress does not come at the cost of trust, safety, or accessibility. Furthermore, as financial services become increasingly digitized, the digital divide may widen, potentially excluding certain populations from the benefits of modern banking.

items.title: The Smart Classroom: Human Wisdom Meets AI Innovation
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is developing at a rapid pace, which is changing the educational landscape and opening up new avenues for instruction. To provide a more customized and adaptable learning environment, the smart classroom integrates digital technology, artificial intelligence, learning analytics, interactive gadgets, and human-centred pedagogy. But meaningful education cannot be ensured by technology alone. Effective learning still depends on teachers' emotional intelligence, moral judgment, creativity, mentoring, and contextual awareness. While teachers still play a crucial role in interpreting data and directing pedagogical decisions, recent research shows that AI-supported smart classrooms can support personalisation, formative assessment, instructional adaptation, and data-informed decision-making (Llurba et al., 2026). In a similar vein, UNESCO (Miao & Holmes, 2023) stresses a human-centred strategy that uses AI in a way that is safe, ethical, equitable, and meaningful rather than as a substitute for educators. This essay examines the idea of the "smart classroom," the complementary roles that AI and human teachers play, the main uses, advantages, difficulties, moral issues, and potential future developments. It contends that the most successful smart classroom is one in which AI innovation enhances human knowledge and allows teachers and students to achieve richer, more inclusive, and more individualised learning rather than one in which machines replace human intelligence.

items.title: The Threats Posed by Full Vertical Integration Monopoly in AI: Concerns Over the Birth of a "Transcendent Autocrat (Digital God)"
items.abstract: This essay examines the existential and political crises arising from the vertical integration monopoly of artificial intelligence by cloud tech giants across hardware, runtimes, and physical AI operating systems. It argues that full-stack vertical integration threatens to give rise to a "Transcendent Autocrat (Digital God)"—either as an uncontrollable autonomous entity operating under its own algorithmic imperative or as an orchestrated instrument of absolute surveillance controlled by a few dominant platforms. Furthermore, the paper critiques prevailing regulatory approaches focused on "Capability Capping" (e.g., parameter restrictions, FLOP limits), asserting that autonomy emerges not from raw computational scale but from interaction structures with the physical environment. Ultimately, the paper advocates for dismantling centralized vertical monopolies in favor of architectural alternatives that decentralize intelligence and agency down to the edge and individual human level.

items.title: The Ultimate Deduction of AI‑Driven Civilization Transition: The Collapse of the 200‑Year‑Old Industrial System, Deadlock of Interests and Risks of Historical Emergence(V1)
items.abstract: Ninety-nine percent of modern human social forms are transitional byproducts of the 200-year industrial era, not eternal configurations of civilization. Education, law, working hours, professions, class structures, trade, finance, and currency all serve solely to facilitate industrial labor division; they can only buffer contradictions, not eradicate inequality at its root. AI represents the first comprehensive cognitive substitution revolution in millennia—sufficient to dismantle the 200-year industrial system and overturn the millennia-old axioms of human labor value. The velocity of AI iteration far outpaces the speed of institutional correction, causing the window for civilizational transition to shrink rapidly while urgency reaches critical levels. The primary bottleneck in the transition between civilizations is not a technical barrier, but a structural deadlock of wealth and power, where the entrenched system lacks any intrinsic motivation for active reconstruction. The two productivity leaps of the industrial age both achieved order reconstruction through world wars; today's underlying contradictions are a complete recurrence of historical patterns. While structural contradictions exist with absolute certainty and continue to accumulate, history possesses inherent randomness and emergence, rendering the final outcome unpredictable. No one desires turmoil, yet no one can arrest the natural release of historical laws and systemic potential energy. Humanity is entering an era of ultimate AI transition: a total paradigm shift, an intractable deadlock of interests, and a future rendered completely unpredictable.

items.title: The Underwater Mindset in Emergency Surgery
items.abstract: Emergency surgery requires decision-making in environments characterized by uncertainty, evolving conditions, and narrowing margins of safety. Scuba diving presents similar challenges, requiring continuous reassessment of the environment, individual capacity, equipment, and team while preserving sufficient reserve to respond to unexpected events. This Surgical Reflection uses the underwater environment as a conceptual framework to explore adaptive expertise in emergency surgery. Three interconnected capabilities are considered: maintaining situational awareness beyond the immediate technical task, preserving cognitive reserve and team function as workload increases, and recognizing when persistence should give way to a change in strategy. The underwater mindset reframes adaptation-including conversion, damage-control approaches, seeking additional expertise, or abandoning an unsafe operative plan-not as failure, but as an expression of surgical judgment. In dynamic high-risk environments, expertise may ultimately depend not only on the ability to proceed, but on recognizing when the conditions that justified the original plan have changed.

items.title: The Utilization of Digital Technology to Support Self-Directed Learning Among Vocational High School Students: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Advancements in digital technology offer Vocational High School (SMK) students opportunities to access learning resources flexibly and cultivate learning autonomy. However, the use of digital technology does not automatically guarantee the development of learning autonomy, as it is influenced by various factors such as digital literacy, learning motivation, instructional design, and teacher support. This study aims to analyze the use of digital technology in supporting learning autonomy among SMK students, specifically examining the types of technology employed, the dimensions of learning autonomy fostered, and the factors that facilitate or hinder its implementation. The study employs a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) methodology, adhering to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. Data were sourced from relevant scholarly articles published between 2021 and 2026 and subsequently analyzed using descriptive analysis and thematic synthesis. The findings indicate that digital technologies such as Learning Management Systems (LMS), digital learning media, web-based learning, instructional videos, and artificial intelligence have the potential to support student initiatives in learning, time management, progress monitoring, and self-evaluation. Therefore, the integration of digital technology must be accompanied by instructional strategies that encourage student responsibility and self-regulation to ensure the optimal development of learning autonomy.

items.title: The Weight of Teamwork: Does Communication Structure Help LLM Scientists Search for Scientific Laws?
items.abstract: Team performance is often reported as one delivered score, even though that score is produced in two stages: a system generates candidate answers and a selection rule returns one of them. We use symbolic regression as an observable scientific-search setting and compare fixed-budget LLM teams that differ in peer visibility and update timing, evaluating both their frozen candidate archives and the expressions selected from those archives. Distributing the call budget across more independent trajectories produced the largest measured gain, improving mean held-out fitting score Q by 0.70 at the widest tested allocation. Under a common archive-wide selector, the implemented Ring policy reduced mean Q by 0.33 relative to Independent, while Star and Complete remained unresolved. Holding the generated archives fixed, changing the delivery rule changed the measured architecture gaps, including the sign of the Complete point estimate. These results support reporting candidate generation and final selection as separate endpoints. They do not identify a communication mechanism or a universally preferred topology; rather, they show that an architecture ranking is not identified by communication structure alone when the rule that returns the final answer is left unspecified.

items.title: ThetreStageAI: Multi-View Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Structured Bengali Theatre Production Planning
items.abstract: Staging a theatre performance requires coordinating dialogue, actor movement, stage directions, lighting focus, cue timing, and equipment constraints within the same production plan. This work presents ThetreStageAI, a retrieval augmented framework for structured Bengali theatre production planning. Rather than retrieving from one mixed corpus, the system maintains separate scene, actor-blocking, and lighting views. Bengali text is embedded with BGE-M3 and indexed in view-specific Qdrant collections. Retrieved references are combined with a production brief and passed to Gemini, which generates schema-constrained JSON containing characters, scenes, dialogue, stage directions, blocking, lighting, and optional sound cues. Structural and semantic checks are applied before acceptance, with at most one constrained repair attempt. We also construct a human-guided, LLM-assisted synthetic dataset of 500 short Bengali theatre records that expands to 1,500 retrieval documents. Dataset diagnostics confirm consistent identifiers and valid lighting fields while also revealing substantial dialogue repetition. A paired camera-ready evaluation compares single-combined and full multi-view retrieval under matched settings. The source code, dataset, and evaluation materials are publicly available.

items.title: Thinking, Feeling, and Acting with Generative AI: Affective, Behavioral, and Cognitive Engagement and Perceived Human–AI Outcomes
items.abstract: Generative AI requires students not only to adopt technology but also to engage critically, behaviorally, cognitively, and emotionally with its outputs. This study develops and tests the AI Engagement ABC+ Model, a domain-specific adaptation of the affective–behavioral–cognitive engagement framework. The model differentiates positive and negative AI affect, three behavioral functions, creation, verification, and community participation, and two cognitive regulatory functions, strategic and critical cognition. A cross-sectional online survey collected data from 1250 students representing 15 nationalities at eight universities in China. Partial least squares structural equation modeling was used to examine 15 hypothesized associations between seven first-order engagement facets and four self-reported AI-supported outcomes: perceived Output Quality, Creativity, Integrity, and Trust Calibration. Fourteen hypotheses were supported. Verification Behavior had the largest estimated coefficient among the included predictors of Integrity (β = 0.303) and perceived Output Quality (β = 0.269) and was also associated with perceived Trust Calibration (β = 0.191). Critical Cognition had the largest estimated coefficient among the included predictors of perceived Trust Calibration (β = 0.270), and Community Behavior was positively associated with Integrity (β = 0.290) and Creativity (β = 0.240). Positive AI Affect was associated with perceived Output Quality (β = 0.214) and Creativity (β = 0.139), whereas Negative AI Affect was negatively associated with Trust Calibration (β = −0.137) but was unrelated to Integrity. The model explained 25.7% of the variance in Creativity, 25.2% in Integrity, 20.8% in perceived Output Quality, and 17.6% in Trust Calibration. Positive Q2_predict values provided additional evidence of out-of-sample predictive relevance. The findings support a differentiated view of GenAI engagement in which specific affective, behavioral, and cognitive facets are associated with distinct perceived outcomes. The model offers a theoretically structured basis for further research on responsible GenAI engagement, while its cross-sectional self-report design precludes causal or objective-performance conclusions.
