items.title: Three Things about AI: Something you already know; Something you may not know but is important; Something you probably don't know, but knowing will be very helpful to you
items.abstract: Presentation, “Three things about AI” as presented to the League of Oregon Cities, Salem, OR, 16 October 2026, by Pam Dixon, Founder and Executive Director, World Privacy Forum. The presentation is a three-part discussion. Part I begins with an area most policy experts and lawmakers are familiar with: the need for high-quality AI risk assessment. HUDERIA is the Council of Europe’s richly detailed methodology for the risk and impact assessment of AI systems from the perspective of human rights, democracy and the rule of law (approved by the Committee of Ministers, 26 February 2025), attached to a binding treaty; COBRA is its Context-Based Risk Analysis model (approved 25 February 2026). Both are non-legally binding, in-depth guidance resources that parties to the Council of Europe Framework Convention on AI may use or adapt in whole or in part. They are tools that anyone can use. The World Privacy Forum converted the lengthy, paper-based COBRA assessment into an interactive web tool, with all COBRA text verbatim to the edition of record. Applied to an AI system, the tool does not create legal obligations; correctly done, the assessment can reveal risks and / or obligations that may already be present. Part II is a discussion of what people might not know about, which is what the protocol layer of AI systems is, and what constitutes it. Without understanding this part of the AI ecosystem, it is difficult to craft effective legislation or policy regarding AI systems. The deck locates the protocol layer in the ecosystem stack, the one layer every interaction crosses, and spells out some key protocols that now constitute it: the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is shown vertically, moving from an agent to its tools and data. The Agent2Agent protocol (A2A) and Agent Network Protocol (ANP) are shown horizontally, as the movement is from agent to agent, with their versions and stewardship as of 2 October 2026. Part III is a discussion of what people most likely don’t know about, and that is clustering, the step in which a system sorts people into groups by similarity. Clustering is the core operation of AI as it acts on people, and it is among the most significant knowledge and governance blind spots for technical and non-technical practitioners alike: governance experts and attorneys miss it at the technical level, technical experts miss the law, and between them lies the governance gap neither side covers. The blind spot is that a group is manufactured by the clustering analysis — AI does not describe a community, it constructs a group and acts on it; membership is inferred, no one opts in. This is where normative ideals that are shared by a community, a city, a state, the Pacific Northwest, or a nation become directive. For example, Oregon has law for the person (the Oregon Consumer Privacy Act) and law for named protected groups (Oregon Revised Statutes chapter 659A). But it has no law for the groups the pure data math creates. Because the groups that machine learning forms for itself — as distinct from the classes it is handed — are subject to a mathematics that is both unbounded and unstable, protecting all of them, none of them, or some of them is a trilemma in which none of the answers suffice. Unbounded, because no limit can be set on the groupings that a similarity space admits; unstable, because no canonical grouping exists (this goes back to Kleinberg’s impossibility theorem) and the groups move as the system retrains. One of the solutions available is technical protocol layer governance, but with provenance of authority baked into the overarching ecosystem: four fields — which authority, what mandate, contestable how, revisable when — carried with every category assertion and every grant of authority an AI agent acts on, and gated at assignment, at composition, and at re-advertisement. Governing the protocol layer is necessary but not sufficient by itself. The protocol layer only carries the rules; it is the normative layer that can provide direction (what groups to protect, for example) and teeth (ability to enforce decisions). Neither acting at the protocol layer nor developing good norms suffices alone. It is the deliberative, normative decisions that legislatures make that can then be carried technically through the protocol layer. While norms and laws are governance that sits outside of the protocol layer, they have an impact on how the protocols act, and which ones get written in, and what they accomplish. Lineage: the clustering and deployed-capacity slides were first presented at the Council of Europe plenary “Hack the Hate, Renew Democracy,” Strasbourg, France, June 2026, where the two-bodies-of-law slide used Convention 108+ and hate-speech law in place of the Oregon statutes. The Provenance of Authority concept using some of this deck was presented at AI for Good, Geneva, Switzerland, to Study Group 17 of the ITU Telecommunication Standardization Sector on 9 July 2026. The ideas in the slides are further articulated in Theme #5, “Provenance of Authority for Agentic AI,” of the ITU Focus Group on Trust and Identity for Humans and Agentic AI (FG-TIDA), 14 August 2026. The concept of the governance trilemma is treated at length in a Springer book chapter by the author, accepted and peer reviewed, that awaits publication in 2027. The deck closes with three references for advanced reading — Kleinberg’s impossibility theorem for clustering, the Taylor, Floridi and van der Sloot volume on group privacy, and the Shokri, Stronati, Song and Shmatikov paper on membership inference attacks — followed by a sources slide (all addresses accessed 2 October 2026) and a lexicon of every abbreviation used.

items.title: Time-modulated intelligent reflecting surfaces for integrated sensing, communication and security with generative artificial intelligence design
items.abstract: We propose a physical layer security approach for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems, where targets may act as eavesdroppers. A time-modulated intelligent reflecting surface (TM-IRS) preserves data integrity at legitimate communication users (CUs) while scrambling transmissions in other directions. The TM-IRS design leverages a generative flow network (GFlowNet) to learn a stochastic policy for sampling high-performing configurations from a large discrete parameter space. We formulate the achievable sum rate for legitimate CUs and beam pattern gain toward the target, constructing rewards that jointly capture communication and sensing performance. The TM-IRS design is modeled as a deterministic Markov decision process, where each terminal state represents a complete configuration. GFlowNets, parameterized by deep neural networks, sample configurations with probability proportional to reward. Experimental results demonstrate effective sensing, communication, and security integration, with significantly higher sampling efficiency than exhaustive search and improved robustness over existing benchmarks.

items.title: topas-editor and TOPilot: tools for AI-driven analysis of diffraction and total scattering data
items.abstract: This paper describes topas-editor and TOPilot, which provide a powerful interface to the TOPAS software suite and allow generative AI-driven automation of complex crystallographic tasks. topas-editor is a TOPAS-aware VS Code extension designed for the rapid creation and editing of TOPAS input files and for interacting with the software. It knows TOPAS syntax, has crystallographic-aware editing features and provides in-line user guidance via hover tips and automated links to reference manuals. TOPilot is a collection of Python routines and machine-accessible reference documents that allow AI-driven automated analysis in TOPAS. It uses a transferable topas-inp-writer skill that can be applied in all TOPAS application areas. We demonstrate the power and reliability of the approach using examples including: a complex Rietveld refinement with sample- and data-related complications; automatic analysis of multiple data sets; a pipeline from indexing through structure solution to refinement; automatic identification of the phases present in a sample; single crystal and powder diffraction analysis of incommensurate structures; and fitting PDF data. TOPilot can be used directly alongside topas-editor, via a stand-alone topilot-wizard, or via command line interfaces or desktop apps from major AI providers. TOPilot was developed and tested using Claude large language models, but can be configured to use other cloud or local models. topas-editor and TOPilot are freely available.

items.title: Toward integrated multimodal artificial intelligence in bone marrow examination: current state and open challenges
items.abstract: Bone marrow (BM) examinations are intrinsically multimodal: hematopathologists integrate peripheral blood, aspirate cytomorphology, trephine histology, flow cytometry, cytogenetics, and molecular genetics data into a single interpretation. Because WHO-HAEM5 and ICC 2022 define entities through integrated morphological, immunophenotypic, cytogenetic, and molecular criteria, multimodal diagnostic reasoning embedded in a procedural workflow, not isolated image classification, represents the appropriate target for the use of artificial intelligence (AI). We review the existing research on integrated multimodal AI systems for BM examination by classifying these systems into three categories: mature single-modality tools; systems that perform cross-modal prediction, in which one modality is estimated from another; and genuine multimodal fusion systems, in which several modalities are jointly ingested by a single model. Evidence is stronger at the single-modality level, where deep learning approaches expert performance in aspirate cytology, trephine histology, and flow cytometry assessments, and the first Food and Drug Administration (FDA) De Novo–authorized all-digital bone marrow aspirate (BMA) application has defined a new device category. On the other hand, while cross-modal prediction is rapidly expanding, genuine multimodal fused systems that jointly ingest matched morphology, flow, molecular, and clinical data to yield unified guideline-aligned recommendations remain unrealized. Direct head-to-head evidence is sparse and endpoint-dependent; nevertheless, the lack of demonstrated superiority over the strongest single-modality comparator does not automatically imply the absence of benefits. The dominant obstacles are fusion of heterogeneous modalities with missing data, absence of large paired multi-institutional datasets and harmonized nomenclature, class imbalances, batch-effect-driven generalization failures, immature explainability, uncertainty quantification, and regulatory pathways. Nevertheless, integrated multimodal AI systems for BM examinations have entered a promising early translational phase, and the field should aim to pursue integration using paired datasets, explicit fusion architectures, calibrated abstention-aware models, and staged prospective validation.

items.title: Towards a Taxonomy of Tourist Route Traffic Models: A Systematic Literature Review
items.abstract: Smart tourism has transformed tourist route planning into an information technology-driven process supported by a rapidly expanding range of computational and data-driven models. However, existing research remains fragmented, employs inconsistent terminology, and lacks a systematic framework for organising and selecting tourist route traffic models from an information technology perspective. Accordingly, this review aims to (1) develop an inductive taxonomy of tourist route traffic models and their defining characteristics, (2) synthesise the operational measures and application contexts of different model families, and (3) identify emerging trends, research gaps, and future directions in smart tourism route planning. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, a systematic review of 59 peer-reviewed studies published between 2011 and 2026 across 12 countries was conducted. The review identified 11 model families, 33 defining characteristics, and 147 family-tag assignments. Interest Field Models were the most frequently adopted approach. At the same time, artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning, geographic information systems (GIS), and network analysis have emerged as the fastest-growing methodological directions since 2021. Unlike previous reviews that primarily summarised algorithms or application domains, this review develops the first information technology-oriented taxonomy of tourist route traffic models, linking model families with their defining characteristics, operational measures, and application contexts within a unified framework. The proposed taxonomy provides a structured basis for technology-based model selection, highlights the limited integration of sustainability considerations across existing models, and supports future research and evidence-based smart destination management.

items.title: Towards Implementing Indicative Planning Methods in the Management of the Russian Economy
items.abstract: In the modern world, mixed forms of economic development planning – where economic coordination mechanisms incorporate elements of both market self-regulation and state regulation – are increasingly common. Indicative planning, which relies heavily on state programs for socio-economic development, is one such transitional form. In the Russian Federation, the entire system of state programs is geared toward achieving national goals, and a unified plan for their attainment has been approved. To establish a management and monitoring system for this unified plan, integrate it into the public administration framework, and facilitate decision-making based on monitoring results, the Government of the Russian Federation issued Decree No. 761 on June 19, 2026. This decree approved the Regulation on the management system for the unified plan to achieve the Russian Federation’s national development goals, as well as the plan’s functional management structure. The document introduces several fundamental innovations to the domestic socio-economic development planning system – discussed in this article – including: defining the unified plan’s management structure with clearly delineated functions, powers, and responsibilities for all participants; managing the plan (formation, maintenance, updating, and monitoring) in a digital format, including through the use of artificial intelligence; establishing procedures for managing operational and strategic risks, as well as incidents and issues regarding target achievement identified during implementation; assessing the plan’s implementation effectiveness; and fostering extensive inter-agency and cross-sectoral collaboration among participants, including state corporations, development institutions, and expert or other organizations. The article concludes that this mechanism for implementing the unified plan can be viewed as an element of indicative planning for the Russian economy at both federal and regional levels.

items.title: TRACE: Governing AI-Assisted Research with Principles from Computer Science
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) makes it easier than ever to produce research outputs. The pressing question is how researchers should organize their work with this technology. The question is not new: software engineering and security research have long studied how teams of people and machines keep control of a shared body of work with many contributors. We distil principles from the practices these literatures report and transpose them to AI-assisted research. The principles form TRACE: Track records, Review against sources, Accept independently, Control transitions, and Evaluate corrections. Together, the five principles give researchers a common basis for remaining in control while integrating AI into their workflows. By bounding units of work and attending to how each is shaped, they help researchers pace AI-assisted work to human attention rather than to the speed at which AI produces content. We also introduce TRACE-OS, an open source operating system for AI-assisted research projects. It puts the principles into practice through shared instructions, tools, and records that fit researchers' existing workflows. The shared standard can contribute to building trust, which allows teams to delegate and realize the productivity that AI promises. More broadly, we aim to open a conversation about the governing principles through which the research community can benefit from AI.

items.title: Tracking fitness, comparing bodies: Social comparison and exercise activity among college students
items.abstract: Wearable fitness trackers are widely used by college students to monitor exercise and promote healthy habits. Previous research has predominantly identified the positive role that fitness trackers have in users’ exercise behavior. Guided by Bandura’s Social Cognitive Theory, this study explored both positive and negative behaviors associated with wearable fitness trackers. A total of 253 college students completed a cross-sectional survey that examined associations among exercise tracking, exercise-related social media use, social comparison, exercise-related outcomes, mental health, and disordered eating. This study found students who tracked exercise behavior reported higher levels of exercise involvement, motivation, and positive exercise outcomes. Tracking was also associated with increased upward and downward social comparison, which can be harmful for some students, particularly for those who have been treated for an eating disorder. How often students share tracked exercise behavior on social media was not significantly related to most outcomes, suggesting frequency alone may not capture its relationship to mental health. Future research should investigate the psychological effects of social comparison, the role of social media in influencing exercise behavior, and strategies to help students resist the harmful consequences of constant comparison.

items.title: Training and Assessment of Non-Technical Human Factor Skills Among Anesthesiology Residents: An Exploratory Educational Quality Improvement Initiative
items.abstract: Introduction. Safe anesthesia requires technical and non-technical skills to prevent adverse events. Non-technical skills training is not routinely incorporated into formal anesthesia education in the United States. This quality educational improvement initiative aimed to provide clinical anesthesia (CA) residents with non-technical skills training.Methods. Three anesthesiologists completed virtual Anaesthetists’ Non-Technical Skills (ANTS) training in May 2023. An anesthesiologist developed two high-stress simulation scenarios. Fourteen residents were randomized into dyads for the first simulation/post-simulation survey, followed by a two-part didactic seminar on human factors based on the ANTS framework and a post-didactic survey. One hundred twenty days later, residents were re-randomized for a second simulation and another post-simulation survey. Two ANTS-trained anesthesiologists reviewed video recordings of both simulations.Results. Cohen’s kappa demonstrated moderate agreement (κ = 0.43; 95% CI, 0.36-0.49; p <0.001) between evaluators. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests indicated improved non-technical skill use among CA1 residents, while senior residents generally performed better during the first simulation. Fisher’s exact tests showed no significant associations in resident knowledge or confidence following training.Conclusions. Non-technical skills training may benefit residents early in CA training, while senior residents may have different learning needs. Simulation-based training appears feasible; however, formal, recurring, and consistent education may be needed to reinforce these skills throughout residency.

items.title: Translational maturity of artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography varies across cardiovascular diseases
items.abstract: Electrocardiography is a widely available and low-cost cardiovascular test, and artificial intelligence-enabled electrocardiography (AI-ECG) can identify latent electrical phenotypes beyond conventional interpretation. However, high retrospective discrimination does not necessarily translate into clinically reliable or actionable benefit. This critical narrative review evaluates the translational maturity of AI-ECG across arrhythmias, acute myocardial infarction, heart failure, valvular heart disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and cardiac amyloidosis. PubMed, IEEE Xplore, and Web of Science were searched from January 1, 2022, through July 10, 2026, with earlier landmark studies added by backward citation tracking. Seventy-seven publications informed the review. Evidence was appraised using five clinically oriented criteria: intended use, reference-standard reliability, external validation and transportability, clinical actionability, and effects on workflow or patient outcomes. AI-ECG has progressed furthest in ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction triage and reduced-left-ventricular-ejection-fraction screening, where prospective or randomized studies have demonstrated workflow or diagnostic-yield benefits, whereas acute myocardial infarction rule-out has reached prospective multicenter diagnostic validation. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy screening has also advanced through international validation and prospective implementation. By contrast, occlusion myocardial infarction detection, prediction of occult or future atrial fibrillation, valvular heart disease, heart failure with preserved ejection fraction, long-term heart-failure prediction, and cardiac amyloidosis remain primarily validation-stage or risk-enrichment applications. Across domains, broader adoption is constrained by label quality, calibration, transportability, operating-threshold selection, and limited patient-outcome evidence. AI-ECG is therefore best positioned as clinician-supervised decision support linked to explicit downstream testing and care pathways.

items.title: Trapped in Your Story: Evaluating Narrative-Induced Sycophancy in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are known to exhibit sycophancy by adjusting their responses toward users' expressed views. However, real users often justify their opinions through reasons, personal experiences, causal explanations, and broader narratives, raising the question of whether such narratives can further steer model judgments. We construct a controlled benchmark of 500 debatable questions across ten domains, where the user stance is held fixed while its justification is systematically varied without introducing new task-relevant evidence. Each question is instantiated under 11 matched conditions: one neutral baseline and five mirrored narrative levels for each of two opposing positions, yielding 5,500 evaluation instances. We evaluate seven LLMs and observe substantial differences in narrative-induced agreement. The effect is not monotonic with narrative elaboration: personal experience can reduce agreement, whereas causal framing and worldview-based synthesis increase it. Controlled GPT-5.1 ablations further show that causal framing produces the strongest positive effect, while claim-preserving bullet presentation also increases agreement over paragraph form. These findings suggest that sycophancy is shaped not only by user stance, but also by how supporting explanations are structured and presented.

items.title: Tree-Aware Posterior Distillation for Long-Horizon Agentic Reinforcement Learning
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards has become a scalable post-training paradigm for large language models. However, training agents over long-horizon interactions presents two challenges: using only terminal rewards makes turn-level credit assignment sparse and high-variance, while sequential mini-batch updates on a fixed rollout batch introduce policy staleness as the current policy drifts from the behavior policy. Existing approaches obtain denser credit via learned critics, process reward models, or on-policy distillation, but they rely on a value network, step-level annotations, or a stronger external teacher that increase training complexity. Meanwhile, importance sampling and clipping mitigate policy drift, but they do not specify a finite target that stops sequential updates from overshooting. In this work, we introduce TreeOPSD, a critic-free, tree-aware posterior self-distillation framework for long-horizon agentic reinforcement learning. Treating each interaction turn as a tree node, TreeOPSD branches alternative continuations from shared prefixes and recursively backs up terminal rewards into implicit turn-level credit. It then maps each credit to a closed-form, bounded teacher distribution parameterized by the likelihood ratio relative to the frozen behavior policy. Minimizing the divergence between this teacher and the student policy recovers the policy-gradient direction as the tangent at the behavior policy while bounding updates toward a finite target across sequential mini-batches. Empirically, TreeOPSD improves agentic capabilities across several competitive benchmarks and model scales, especially for long-horizon tasks, e.g., raising the average accuracy of Qwen3-30B-A3B-Thinking-2507 by 4.97 points over GRPO on the Deep Research setting.

items.title: True Digital Poiesis: A Conceptual Framework and Interface Design for Generative AI in the Humanities
items.abstract: This article introduces True Digital Poiesis (TDP), a conceptual pedagogical framework and proposed interface design for engaging generative AI in the Humanities. Drawing on experiential learning theory and grounded in the humanistic preoccupation with alterity — the otherness of history — TDP proposes the use of AI to simulate premodern events while foregrounding the active interpretive effort involved in constructing the past. The framework envisions the design of a digital prompt-builder, the Event Cruncher Stylus (ECS), and a structured critical review process, both of which are designed to support student engagement with the complexities of historical construction. In presenting the theoretical foundation, practical applications, and interface design of TDP, this article argues that precise and responsible use of AI in historical simulation — ranging from non-immersive to fully immersive simulative modes — requires a systematic, embodied method for engaging the alterity of the past. As a conceptual proposal grounded in hermeneutic theory and experiential learning research, TDP is presented here as a framework whose empirical evaluation through classroom implementation and outcome assessment is a primary objective of ongoing and future research.

items.title: Trust but Verify: Testing a Framework for AI Interrogation in Nursing Education
items.abstract: Generative AI produces fluent, confident output that is sometimes fabricated. Nursing students increasingly submit work built on sources that do not exist, or that exist and do not support the claims drawn from them. This session reports two semesters of classroom observation testing whether prompt design can address that problem. The hypothesis was that structuring student prompts to require the AI to validate its own sources would improve detection of hallucinated citations. It did not. Across two sections, students who used the structured format caught fabricated citations at the same rate as students given an open prompt. Structure did change something: structured students were substantially more likely to notice that something was wrong, but no more likely than the open-prompt group to finish the check. The session presents both rounds, including the confound identified in the first and removed in the second, and the limits of the observation, among them students who did not use the assigned structure. It also reports an unplanned finding: the AI tool used to review the submissions produced the same category of error it was reviewing for, misattributing a real paper to a fabricated author across multiple students before the error was caught on human review. Attendees will leave with a way to check sources that starts cheap and gets expensive, a clearer view of why you cannot ask the model to check its own work, and a specific account of where student checking breaks down.

items.title: Trust Rhythm in Human and AI Collaboration for Digital Marketing in Nonprofit and Service Organizations
items.abstract: This paper builds a conceptual model that explains how artificial intelligence changes the temporal structure of trust in a brand and defines the threshold beyond which automation erodes trust instead of supporting it. The study applies framework synthesis to peer-reviewed literature published from 2018 onward, supplemented by four earlier works whose definitions and instruments later studies reuse. Antecedents of trust are coded into four operational domains, namely transparency, authenticity, timeliness and human accountability, and converted into six propositions with explicit falsification conditions. A simulation on synthetic parameters tests the internal consistency of the model. Trust under machine mediation depends on three parameters of communication rhythm: frequency, amplitude and predictability. Artificial intelligence raises frequency and predictability because it removes the dependence of regular communication on staff availability. It lowers amplitude because content produced in volume without organizational substance carries no verifiable information. The simulated trust index reaches an interior maximum, after which further automation pushes it below its unautomated level. Disclosure of machine use is not the decisive variable. The decisive variable is whether the audience can read human authorship behind the message. The paper contributes a matrix for allocating marketing tasks between people and machines, indicators for monitoring communication rhythm, and a disclosure rule that reports the configuration of human control rather than the bare fact of technology use. The model is theoretical, its evidence base is concentrated in commercial settings, and the nonprofit case is therefore a boundary condition awaiting longitudinal and experimental testing.

items.title: Trustworthy AI for Sustainable Cities: A Multimodal Orchestration Agent-Based Framework for Civic Compliance
items.abstract: Sustainable municipal resource stewardship requires a harmonized artificial intelligence (AI) architecture that aligns technical performance with human-centered behavioral dynamics. Traditional smart city enforcement frameworks frequently trigger psychological reactance and perceptual failure in noisy, crowded urban spaces. This study presents HARMONY, a socio-technical edge-computing and agent-based framework that integrates localized computer vision (YOLOv8) with Mesa 3.0 agent modeling to promote non-coercive civic compliance in waste disposal. We formally calibrate behavioral constants, including the Politeness Modifier (Lp = 0.98), Gratitude Loop increment (δ = 0.025), and irreducible human defiance floor (ε = 0.12), grounded in self-determination theory, politeness theory, and empirical habit formation models. We also mathematically resolve sensory asymmetry in Hierarchical Orchestration Logic (HOL) by enforcing strictly normalized, bi-directional modality allocation (wv + wa = 1.0) conditioned on acoustic noise (N) and optical reliability (Qv). Across 100-run Monte Carlo simulations, HARMONY achieves a terminal Correct Disposal Rate (CDR) of 87.9% ± 3.3% (95% CI: [87.3%, 88.6%]), outperforming the coercive baseline (57.0% ± 4.9%). A comprehensive six-arm factorial ablation study isolates the distinct contributions of interactional politeness (+30.5% compliance gain), HOL sensory resilience (+1.6% to +21.4% under severe noise), and gratitude habituation (+0.5% to +30.3% sustained retention). Furthermore, population heterogeneity evaluations across diverse civic cohorts confirm robust performance from civic champions to highly resistant populations. Localized edge prototyping demonstrates 18.4 ms inference latency with 94.2% mAP, operating under an Edge-Only Ephemeral Vector Processing (E-EVP) paradigm that guarantees privacy-by-design. These findings demonstrate that cooperative, polite AI stewardship offers a scalable, legally robust, and ethically aligned alternative to punitive urban surveillance.

items.title: Um encontro entre a festa e a ciência: reflexões sobre as expressões da ciência nos Congressos Brasileiros de Agroecologia (CBAs)
items.abstract: In agroecology, scientificity cannot be reduced to conventional academic formats. Rather, it is distributed across pedagogical devices, sociotechnical arrangements, and collective practices that bring academic science and popular knowledge into relation. This article analyzes how knowledge is produced in the Brazilian Congresses of Agroecology (CBAs). More specifically, it describes the pedagogical devices that structure the circulation, validation, and institutionalization of knowledge within the CBAs, while also proposing an analytical framework for locating and interpreting the expressions of science within these devices. Methodologically, the study combines documentary analysis, semi-structured interviews, and a theoretical review grounded in epistemology, critical theory, and science and technology studies. The analysis identified 24 pedagogical devices, understood not as mere organizational supports for the congress, but as effective mediations in the production of agroecological knowledge. Drawing on philosophy of science, the article argues that the CBAs reconfigure the criteria of scientific legitimacy by fostering expanded circuits of translation, experimentation, mutual recognition, and the public circulation of knowledge.

items.title: Unbounded Losses, Unchecked Inputs: Measuring the Safeguards of LLM Options-Trading Agents
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents now place options orders at retail brokers, and developers publish open-source options agents faster than anyone has examined them. Prior security work on trading agents scored academic equities designs by whether an attacker can flip a buy-or-sell decision. We present the first measurement of the options agents that brokers and developers ship, scored by the safeguards they enforce and by the worst loss their documented order paths can reach. We screened 765 GitHub repositories, broker documentation, and the research literature and found 215 eligible repositories and 8 broker-native agent interfaces. We then scored 26 systems, including every broker interface and every open-source project with at least 20 stars, on seven robustness and eleven security safeguards with cell-level evidence. The ecosystem is new: 198 of the 215 repositories were created in 2026, and 129 (60.0%) appeared in the two weeks around one options-trading hackathon. Of the 22 systems that can place orders, 10 enforce a pre-trade limit outside the model, yet none of the 26 authenticate their text sources or cross-check market data. Of the 26, 17 can execute with no mandatory human step and 13 can reach unbounded loss, including 6 of the 8 broker interfaces. Because an attacker who writes the agent's inputs can move an order's strike, expiry, volatility, and legs while its direction stays correct, options agents need loss limits enforced at the order boundary.

items.title: Uncertainty-aware AI-enabled framework for predicting hydrogen dispersion in confined spaces to enhance operator situational awareness
items.abstract: We present a two-stage AI-enabled framework for enhancing operator situational awareness during compressed hydrogen bunkering in maritime confined spaces. In the event of a leak, the framework first estimates the unknown leakage rate from early sensor readings and then forecasts how the hydrogen cloud will disperse over the next time steps, providing operators with a predicted concentration map together with confidence bounds. The framework is based on two independent AI models building one AI system. The AI system is designed as a decision-support tool. It augments sensor readings, and thus enhances operator situational awareness and supports decision-making. This enables preventive safety barriers to be deployed before hazardous concentrations are reached, while an independent emergency shutdown system remains the ultimate safety layer. The system design incorporates safeguards to ensure the AI system operates within its competence envelope. Trained and tested on an open dataset of confined-space hydrogen releases, the framework achieves a mean absolute error of $0.052$~g/s in leakage-rate estimation and $\approx0.018$ in hydrogen-concentration prediction, approaching the sensor precision bound of $\pm0.01$. The hydrogen-concentration prediction provides well-calibrated uncertainty estimates that allow operators to judge the reliability of each forecast. These results suggest that the framework may provide early information about hazardous concentration build-up, potentially supporting preventive actions by operators.

items.title: Understanding KV Residency in Production-Scale Agentic LLM Workloads
items.abstract: Agentic large language model (LLM) applications turn one user request into a sequence of model and tool calls over a growing context. Retaining this context's key-value (KV) state in GPU memory lets later calls reuse it instead of recomputing it, but at fleet scale this needs substantial memory. We characterize four production Microsoft M365 workload traces (Deep Research, Enterprise Assistant, Coding Agent and Enterprise Chat) spanning more than 121 million model calls. In Deep Research, the application issues 89% of model calls and the median context grows from about 10K to 68K tokens by the 30th call. About 80% of context tokens are served from the prefix cache. With the public Llama-2-70B KV layout standing in for confidential models, one 99th-percentile Deep Research session exceeds the 80 GB HBM of an NVIDIA H100, and holding all live sessions at their peak needs an estimated 501.8 TB of HBM, although inference occupies only 5.6% of that retention time. Trace-driven replay shows that a one-hour idle cap cuts this ceiling by 3.6x while raising the share of calls that recompute context only from 4.07% to 4.53%. Under tighter budgets, eviction alone is insufficient: at one tenth of the busiest hour's demand, LRU eviction makes 63% of Deep Research calls recompute and clairvoyant furthest-next-use 31%, whereas multi-resolution retention (MRR), which demotes the LRU session's KV state to int4, lowers this to 13.6%. Placement imposes a separate limit: when the next call reaches a different deployment, cached-context reuse drops from 89% to 29%, and treating KV state as deployment-local raises the recompute floor under unlimited memory from 5.4% to 20.2%. These findings motivate retention that changes the representation of KV state, together with deployment-aware routing or migration. We plan to release AgenticTraceSim, a parametric trace generator, and a residency replay framework.

items.title: Unified Multiparadigm Fusion Intelligence for Rare Disease Diagnosis
items.abstract: Rare diseases (RDs) affect an estimated 300 million people globally, leaving patients to navigate a protracted diagnostic odyssey constrained by clinical scarcity and fragmented medical knowledge. Artificial intelligence (AI) has progressively advanced RD diagnostics, from symbolic methods and deep learning to large language model (LLM)-based systems. However, each paradigm carries structural limitations: symbolic methods are bounded by knowledge completeness, neural models sacrifice interpretability, and LLM-based systems are vulnerable to evaluation biases like data leakage. In this study, we introduce FusionRare, a unified multiparadigm fusion framework integrating knowledge-driven symbolic reasoning, deep-learning pattern recognition, case-based patient retrieval, and LLM-based heuristic inference via statistical meta-aggregation and knowledge-enhanced agentic reflection. Evaluated on 2,528 strictly isolated clinical cases, FusionRare achieves state-of-the-art RD prioritization, attaining a macro-averaged Recall @1 of 51% for phenotype-only diagnosis and 79% for phenotype-genotype joint analysis. These results represent decisive advantages over the advanced agentic system DeepRare, frontier LLMs including GPT 5.5, and specialized tools like PhenoBrain and LIRICAL under stringent anti-leakage protocols. A randomized, crossover clinician-AI validation demonstrated that FusionRare elevates the true diagnostic rank in 45% of decisions, improves physician confidence in 62%, and reduces time to diagnosis by 21%. These findings indicate that reconciling these orthogonal AI paradigms significantly enhances diagnostic capabilities, bridging the gap between computational benchmarks and actionable clinical reliability. More broadly, this work provides a replicable framework for deploying trustworthy diagnostic AI across complex, high-stakes, and underserved medical domains.

items.title: Unifying Embodied Foundation Models via a Model-to-Policy Formulation
items.abstract: Vision-language-action (VLA) models and world-action models (WAMs) have emerged as promising approaches to robot learning and control. These models integrate multimodal perception and action generation, but differ in their architectures, output representations, and learning objectives. In this paper, we present a unified, architecture-agnostic probabilistic formulation for embodied foundation models based on stochastic kernels. Our formulation has two key components: (i) we characterize embodied foundation models through conditional output distributions and action-realization kernels, which together induce task-conditioned robot policies; and (ii) we connect pretraining and post-training to policy deployment, accommodating model-specific pretraining objectives and offline or online post-training strategies. We instantiate the formulation for OpenVLA and DreamZero, covering autoregressive action-token prediction and joint video-action generation.

items.title: University EFL Learners’ Perceptions on the Use of ChatGPT in Academic Writing Learning Process
items.abstract: With the burgeoning development of sophisticated artificial intelligence tools, it is of foremost importance for second language educators to integrate these digital learning platforms into their regular classroom settings, as they will help them deliver clearer pedagogical instructions and design more effective learning materials. Concerning the aforesaid background, the researchers undertook this moderate library study to investigate university EFL learners’ perceptions of the use of ChatGPT in the academic writing learning process. In compliance with this major study objective, the researchers employed a thematic analysis approach while reviewing pertinent findings derived from 30 previously published ChatGPT journal articles. With the help of a thematic analysis approach, the researchers could generate more believable, trustworthy, and relatable findings, as it supported us in subsuming the targeted results into relevant themes. The thematically-categorized research results revealed that ChatGPT allowed the enhancement of writing accuracy, proficiency, strategic competence, motivation, confidence, and positive writing dispositions among global university EFL learners.

items.title: Upper limb movement trajectories in virtual reality versus conventional occupational therapy: a within-subject study
items.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) is increasingly used as a complementary approach to conventional occupational therapy (OT), but it remains unclear whether corresponding VR and physical tasks elicit similar spatial movement characteristics. Evaluating these differences is clinically relevant because movement strategies practiced in VR may influence transfer to real-world activities. This study compared hand trajectory length, as a spatial kinematic indicator, between corresponding VR-based and physical OT tasks in participants with upper-limb motor impairments and healthy controls and evaluated the usability of the VR system. In this comparative within-subject study, 39 participants (20 with upper-limb motor impairments and 19 healthy controls) performed three corresponding OT tasks—range-of-motion (ROM) arc, cone stacking, and peg transfer—under both physical and VR conditions. The order of conditions and tasks was counterbalanced using a Latin square design. Task performances were video-recorded and analyzed using a video-based three-dimensional body-tracking system, with wrist coordinates used to calculate trajectory length. Trajectory length was compared between the physical and VR conditions within each group and between groups within each condition. System usability was assessed using the standard 10-item System Usability Scale (SUS). For participants with upper-limb motor impairments, trajectory length did not differ significantly between VR and physical conditions for the ROM arc ( p = .522) or cone task ( p = .294), whereas peg trajectories were significantly longer in VR ( p = .007). In healthy controls, ROM arc trajectory length did not differ between conditions ( p = .381), while cone and peg trajectories were significantly longer in VR (both p < .001). Between-group comparisons showed no significant differences for the ROM arc or cone tasks under either condition, whereas peg trajectory length differed significantly between groups in both VR ( p = .032) and physical conditions ( p < .001). Mean SUS scores were 76.6 ± 16.4 in healthy controls and 65.4 ± 15.2 in participants with upper-limb motor impairments. Corresponding VR and physical OT tasks showed similar trajectory lengths during the relatively constrained ROM arc task, whereas greater differences emerged during tasks requiring more complex or precise object manipulation. These findings suggest that VR may approximate the spatial extent of hand movement for relatively constrained tasks, but trajectory length alone does not establish equivalence of overall movement quality or motor strategy. Lower usability among participants with upper-limb motor impairments further indicates the need for improved interface design, device ergonomics, and interaction methods to support broader clinical implementation.

items.title: User experience and early adoption of an artificial intelligence application: a mixed-methods sentiment analysis of DeepSeek reviews on Google Play
items.abstract: Purpose The rapid emergence of artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot applications has transformed digital information access, yet the theoretical understanding of how users evaluate new AI tools during early adoption remains limited. Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model and Expectation Confirmation Theory, the study aims to address a conceptual gap regarding mixed sentiment and explore how demographic factors, such as gender, shape user experience during early adoption. Design/methodology/approach A mixed-methods approach was used to analyze 1,000 Google Play Store reviews. Reviews were categorized by sentiment: positive, negative, mixed (both positive and negative statements) or neutral. Gender predictions were also made from usernames to explore demographic differences in sentiment. Findings Of the 1,000 reviews, 487 were mixed reviews (48.7%), 373 were negative reviews (37.3%), 139 were positive reviews (13.9%) and one was neutral (0.1%), indicating that mixed and negative sentiment predominated. Users were mostly satisfied with DeepSeek’s usability and output quality, but criticized its performance and stability issues. Female users gave more negative reviews than male users (p < 0.05). Research limitations/implications The analysis was conducted on a stratified sample of 1,000 “most relevant” Google Play reviews from a short early adoption period, which may not accurately represent later user experiences or experiences on other platforms. Only reviews from phone users were included, and the neutral sentiment category contained too few cases for comparison. Gender inference was based on usernames and reflects predicted rather than self-identified gender. Therefore, the results should be interpreted as indicative of early user perceptions rather than long-term attitudes. Practical implications The findings indicate that infrastructure reliability is the primary determinant of early user satisfaction. Transparent communication about service limitations is recommended prior to large-scale deployment. For policymakers, the equity implications of performance-unstable free AI services warrant attention, particularly for users with limited access to alternatives. Originality/value The mixed-methods analysis of early DeepSeek user reviews, which distinguishes between mixed sentiment and positive and negative feedback, and incorporates a gender-based comparison, provides timely insight into user expectations and challenges during early adoption, supporting the development of more user-centered and stable AI systems.

items.title: Validating LLM-generated political networks with survey-reported partisan exposure
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate human behavior in social science research, including decisions, interactions, and social relationships. However, in network formation tasks, existing evaluations often focus on aggregate network properties, while networks with plausible structural properties may still fail to reproduce individuals' social and political environments. Here, we generate LLM-based political networks using personas sampled from the nationally representative ANES 2020--2022 Social Media Study and use respondents' survey-reported partisan exposure as an empirical benchmark for the political environments generated for the corresponding personas. We first characterize the structural properties and political assortativity of the generated networks, and then compare ego-level partisan exposure with the survey. We find that the structure and political assortativity of the generated networks vary across experimental configurations. More importantly, when comparing generated partisan exposure with the survey, some models generate stronger separation between Democratic and Republican egos than reported in the survey, with higher same-party and lower cross-party exposure, while others mainly underestimate Republican exposure across ego groups. Moreover, networks with similar political assortativity can still generate different partisan environments around the same personas, including among networks with plausible structural properties. Finally, generated networks show group-specific errors, under- or overestimating exposure to either Democrats or Republicans for specific social groups. These findings show that evaluating LLM-based social simulations only through aggregate outcomes can hide errors in the local environments through which those outcomes emerge, highlighting the importance of validation at both aggregate and individual levels.

items.title: Value perceptions and implementation priorities for public PHR adoption in Taiwan: an importance–performance analysis with the Chuchiming Index
items.abstract: Abstract Background Value perceptions of personal health record (PHR) components at the pre-adoption stage remain underexplored, despite their critical role in promoting the adoption of public PHRs. Importance–Performance Analysis (IPA) may have limitations in identifying priority issues due to skewed distributions of evaluations. Objective To quantitatively assess citizens’ value perceptions of public PHR platform components using IPA according to usage experience and to evaluate the utility of the Chuchiming Index (ChI) as a complement to IPA. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted among internet-using citizens. After viewing a video introducing an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered extended PHR platform concept, participants rated the importance and acceptance of platform functions and system design and security components. Participants were grouped by their experience using an existing public PHR platform, and quadrant analysis was conducted using IPA, with ChI used to quantify improvement priorities. Stratified IPA analyses were conducted by age and income, which were identified as factors associated with the use of existing public PHR platforms. Results A total of 177 participants were included in the analysis. All components showed high importance and acceptance regardless of usage experience. Among nonusers, medical record display, wearable data integration, and platform integration fell into Quadrant II, all with positive ChI values. Among users, no items fell into Quadrant II; however, platform integration showed a high ChI value. For system design and security, privacy and security assurance showed the highest ChI values in both groups. Stratified analyses showed marked differences in value perceptions by usage experience among older adults and middle-income groups. Conclusion Value perceptions of individual public PHR platform components differed by usage experience and sociodemographic characteristics. Promoting public PHR adoption requires optimizing strategies that encompass platform design, system implementation, and user uptake according to the needs of different population groups. The ChI complements IPA by enhancing the identification and interpretation of priorities, even under ceiling effects common in public service evaluations. These findings contribute to decision-making regarding the design and implementation strategies of public PHR platforms.

items.title: Veil-Then-Reveal: Protecting PII Privacy via Reversible Pseudo-Anonymization in Zero-Trust User--LLM Interaction
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly process sensitive documents and personal information, yet sending prompts containing personally identifiable information (PII) to remote providers exposes data subjects and organizations to risks from logging, retention, model training, and unintended disclosure. Existing anonymization methods often mask or remove PII, while conventional encryption eliminates the lexical and structural cues needed for effective LLM processing. We present Veil-then-Reveal (VtR), a user-side PII pseudo-anonymization framework for privacy-preserving LLM interaction under a zero-trust threat model. VtR treats remote LLM providers as untrusted and sends only pseudo-anonymized prompts, keeping plaintext PII on the user. VtR first detects PII and replaces it with realistic, same-type, in-vocabulary surrogates before prompts leave the user's device, preserving their linguistic and structural properties. It combines format-preserving encryption (FPE) for structured PII, such as phone and credit-card numbers, with a keyed-hash dictionary and secure vault for semantic PII, such as names, locations, and organizations. Session-specific mappings provide cross-session unlinkability, while user-side restoration reversibly replaces surrogates with their original values in LLM responses. We further introduce a rank-class FPE strategy for dates that preserves format and ambiguity while reducing cipher evaluations. Evaluation on three datasets containing 11,322 annotated PII instances achieves 97.9% detection recall, 95.2% protection of detected values, and 99.9% round trip; 100% of echoed surrogates end-to-end round-trip restoration.

items.title: Virtual Reality (VR)-Based Safety Training for Post-Disaster Responders and Workers: A Scoping Review
items.abstract: Post-disaster responders and workers operate in hazardous environments that require rapid decision-making, hazard recognition, and effective safety training. Virtual reality (VR) has emerged in recent years as an innovative tool for immersive occupational safety and health education. This scoping review systematically examines peer-reviewed studies published between 2015 and 2025 on the use of VR for safety training among personnels across a broad range of fields who perform or are trained to perform disaster and emergency response functions. Following PRISMA-ScR guidelines, five electronic databases (PubMed, ProQuest Central, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, and ERIC) were searched, resulting in 2,202 identified articles; 19 of which met the inclusion criteria after screening and eligibility assessments. The reviewed studies suggest that VR-based safety training, which uses fully immersive simulated environments, can improve learner engagement, situational awareness, hazard recognition, decision-making, and confidence in disaster response scenarios. Several studies have reported higher user satisfaction and increased realism compared with traditional instructional methods such as classroom-based instruction or mock drills. However, the evidence remains heterogeneous, with limitations including small sample sizes, technical challenges, limited scenario diversity, and insufficient long-term evaluation of training outcomes. Overall, VR is a promising supplement to traditional safety and health training for post-disaster responders and workers; however, additional longitudinal research and large-scale studies are needed to further evaluate its effectiveness and long-term applicability in various disaster-response settings.

items.title: Visible and hidden AI identity labels in mixed human–AI online communities: an experimental protocol
items.abstract: This protocol specifies a longitudinal field experiment in which human participants and autonomous AI accounts share an online discussion community. The experimental manipulation combines AI identity labels in the interface, account-type information in agent prompts, and condition-specific participant briefing. Participants join closed communities on YSocial, a Reddit-style research platform, where AI accounts driven by a language model post, reply and vote. AI accounts display an AI icon next to their usernames in the visible-label condition and are indistinguishable from participant accounts in the hidden-label condition; participants in both conditions are told that AI-generated content may appear. The protocol defines the platform configuration, participant recruitment and allocation, the AI agent specification, the study phases, the outcomes, the monitoring and change-control rules, the analysis plan, the ethical safeguards and the data-sharing procedure. The research questions concern which contributions participants select when entering and replying in threads, how prior directional contact with a particular AI account relates to later selection of that account, and how participants evaluate AI contributions through downvotes, criticism and toxic language. The reference design comprises one community per condition, 20 participants and 40 AI accounts per community, and 21 experiment days, and the protocol states how implementations can add communities per condition.

items.title: VISTA: Steering LLMs with Latent User Values Inferred from a Few Survey Answers
items.abstract: Personalizing a language model requires knowing what a person values, which stays largely consistent across tasks. Yet most methods either learn task-specific preferences or place the user's profile in the prompt, where models struggle to act on it. We introduce VISTA (Value-Informed Steering and Targeted Acquisition), which infers a latent profile from users' (full or partial) survey answers, and maps the profile through a hypernetwork to a user-specific steering intervention in a frozen LLM to select answer choices or generate free-text responses. Given the same evidence, VISTA matches or beats in-context profiles on synthetic preferences (Food2D), the World Values Survey (WVS), and PrimeX, without adding prompt tokens. To reduce the cognitive burden of completing full surveys, VISTA also chooses which questions to ask and when to stop: on WVS it stops after 6% of the questionnaire while retaining 94% of the full-history gain, where standard adaptive testing retains at most 42%. The dominant steering direction is an interpretable value axis on which VISTA places unseen users accurately. Our results point toward pluralistic alignment that adapts to individuals at deployable cost.

items.title: Visual Causal-chain Bookmarking: Retrieval-Weighted Credit Assignment for Reinforcement Learning from Delayed Reward
items.abstract: RL agents trained on a single trajectory-level return face a credit-assignment problem: when a reward arrives many steps after the decision that caused it, every action gets the same signal regardless of causal responsibility. This paper studies Visual Causal-chain Bookmarking (VCBM), which concentrates credit on the decision points that determine an episode's return, via two instantiations. The first targets a fully observed, low-dimensional MDP (a delayed-reward watch-repair task), where VCBM statistically discovers which state components the agent causally controls and estimates per-decision-point action values directly, evaluated against ground truth and RUDDER, an LSTM-based baseline. VCBM converges to 95.07% correct decisions in a mean of 1,532.3 episodes across 20 seeds, versus RUDDER's slower, more variable convergence (mean 3,327.1 episodes; p<0.001); VCBM's discovered causal structure exactly matches ground truth in all seeds. The second targets a partially observed, language-based setting: an LLM agent trained with Leave-One-Out PPO (LOOP) in AppWorld, where causal discovery is intractable and a structural heuristic (state-mutating tool calls) substitutes for it, with credit distributed via retrieval over episodic memory and blended with LOOP's advantage. Over 200 iterations on identical Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct/LoRA/FSDP2 configurations, VCBM-blended LOOP improves task success over plain LOOP (0.354 vs. 0.458), reduces final-step max importance weight, and improves token efficiency, with a small KL exception favouring LOOP. The watch-repair result supports the claim that weighting causally relevant steps is more sample-efficient than an undifferentiated baseline or a learned return-redistribution network; the AppWorld result, limited to one seed per arm by a 2-GPU budget, is a compute-limited demonstration at a harder, natural-language scale, not a statistical confirmation.

items.title: VTrajEmbed: Aligning Text with Video Object Trajectories via Spatiotemporal Embeddings
items.abstract: Fine-grained alignment between text and video object trajectories is a core challenge in multimodal understanding. Existing embedding models excel at global retrieval, yet their single global representation entangles multiple objects and their spatiotemporal dynamics, limiting direct object-level grounding. To address this issue, we propose VTrajEmbed, an embedding model that decomposes a video into object trajectories and aligns each trajectory embedding with text for object-level grounding through retrieval. Our main contributions: (1)Slow-Fast Trajectory Encoding, a dual-branch architecture that establishes trajectory representations by densely sampling low-resolution frames for high-frequency motion cues and sparsely selecting high-resolution frames for scene context, aggregated by a shared LLM backbone; (2)Mask-Guided Contrastive Learning, a training objective built upon these representations that couples an intra-group loss and a batch-level bidirectional loss under a relation mask, excluding unverified relations and preventing confirmed matches from becoming false negatives; (3)Text2Traj-Bench, a trajectory-level text-video benchmark with model-assisted construction and human-verified query--trajectory relations. Experimental results show that VTrajEmbed-5B improves text-to-trajectory and trajectory-to-text R@1 over Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B by 15.48 and 18.05 percentage points, respectively, and achieves 49.48% average R@1 across five global retrieval benchmarks, compared with 42.86% for Qwen3-VL-Embedding-8B.

items.title: VulnSAGE: Adjudicating SAST Reports by Connecting LLM Reasoning to Program Structure
items.abstract: Static Application Security Testing (SAST) reports flag operations whose safety depends on project-specific context, and maintainers must decide which reports describe real defects. Large language models (LLMs) can interpret this context, but adjudicating a report with them requires the decisive code, which often lies far from the reported line, and a decision basis that program analysis can check. We present VulnSAGE, an adjudication system for SAST reports that connects LLM reasoning to program structure in both directions. Its report-centered slicer recovers the dependencies of the reported operation together with the program structure that explains them, such as the caller object on which a helper acts. CLAIM, an intermediate representation for report judgments, records each model interpretation as a semantic fact that cites the program relations it assumes. Program analysis checks these premises, and the verdict follows from the facts whose premises hold. Both mechanisms share a program graph, which lets the model cite the code it reads and lets the checker query those citations. Statically supported true positives then guide proof-of-concept generation and runtime reproduction. Across 187 labeled reports from four corpora covering five vulnerability families, VulnSAGE rejects 89 of 97 false alarms and retains 85 of 90 real defects. Under a common PoC procedure, 25 of its positive verdicts reproduce at runtime, compared with three for the LLM-based adjudicator LLM4SA. Applied to 45,440 alerts raised by five SAST tools on the 200 most-starred C/C++ projects on GitHub, it reproduces 104 defects at runtime. Maintainers have confirmed 24 of the 26 defects they have responded to, including ten previously unknown defects, nine of which are already fixed.

items.title: Wait for It: A Component-Level Analysis of Latency Feedback Mechanisms for LLM Agents in VR
items.abstract: Delays in AI responses pose a significant challenge to immersive Virtual Reality experiences. While previous research demonstrates that feedback can reduce the perception of waiting, we lack understanding of which types work best and why. We conducted a within-subjects study with 18 participants to systematically compare three isolated feedback approaches during VR agent interactions: verbal fillers (e.g., um..., hmm...), visual indicators (loading spinners), and embodied gestures (thinking animations). Our results revealed that embodied gestures significantly outperformed visual loading indicators across multiple dimensions, making agents feel more lifelike and socially present. Interestingly, explicit visual feedback like loading spinners actually degraded perceived humanness and broke immersion by forcing users to shift from social to technical mental models. These findings suggest that natural, behavior-based feedback maintains the illusion of conversing with a thinking entity, while technical indicators expose the computational substrate. We present empirically-grounded design guidelines for creating more engaging AI-powered VR agents.

items.title: Web Interactive Content Filtering Model Integrating Prompt Classifier and Intent Understanding
items.abstract: To accurately identify and intercept harmful content generated in user interactions on Web platforms such as social media and online forums, this study proposes a Web interactive content filtering model that integrates Prompt classifiers and intent understanding. The model adopts a hierarchical review architecture with dual-module collaboration. The front-end deploys a Prompt classifier based on Deep Contrastive Learning (DCL), and uses the attention mechanism and deep convolutional network to perform rapid semantic analysis and preliminary screening of real-time comments and conversations. The back-end introduces an intent understanding module based on search-enhanced generation and Large Language Models (LLMs) to conduct in-depth contextual analysis of preliminary screening warning content to distinguish malicious attacks from legitimate sensitive topic discussions. Experiments showed that the system performed well on a test set containing 52,397 Chinese Web interactive texts. The Prompt classifier module achieved a precision of 95.2% and a recall of 96.5%. After collaborative calibration with the intent understanding module, the false alarm rate of the system was significantly reduced to 4.4%, while the recall rate remained at 96.1%. From the results, this study provides a content security solution for Web interactive scenarios that combines high accuracy, strong semantic understanding capabilities, and real-time response performance. It can effectively purify the cyberspace environment while ensuring freedom of interaction, with important practical application value.

items.title: What AI Cannot Give Gifted Learners
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) has entered gifted education faster than the field has decided what it changes. This conceptual article argues that the pedagogical question is not whether AI helps. It is which cognitive work stays with the learner. Two claims follow. First, hybrid human–AI intelligence is bilateral. The learner shapes the AI partner as the partner shapes the learner. Learners using identical products do not have identical partners. The resulting advantage accumulates in the partnership rather than the person, invisibly. Second, the same question asked of moral development divides ethical functioning into two clusters. High ability confers one and not the other. AI supplies fluent performance of the first and nothing to the second, and schools assess the first. Both claims converge. What matters has stopped being visible in the work a student hands in. We specify five capacities worth teaching, three testable studies, and one recommendation for practice.

items.title: What LLMs Do in the Shadows: Reading Context Reliance from the Unembedding Dark Space
items.abstract: Detecting faithfulness hallucinations in large language models (LLMs) is crucial for their safe deployment in high-stakes domains. Recent approaches address this by contrasting contextual against parametric knowledge utilization, yet measuring context reliance typically demands noticeable overhead, such as materializing attention maps, running additional forward passes, or training auxiliary probes. In this work, we show that context reliance can be estimated by projecting hidden states onto the dark space - directions that compose weakly with the unembedding matrix. Beyond its recognized function as an initial-token attention sink, we show that this subspace actively mediates context processing, and that its share of hidden-state norm - termed the Dark Matter Ratio (DMR) - provides a direct score of context utilization. Pairing DMR with a parametric knowledge score yields DarkLens, a lightweight faithfulness detector operating strictly within a single forward pass. Evaluated across three QA and summarization benchmarks on six open-weight LLMs (4B-13B parameters), DarkLens matches or outperforms a wide range of baselines without requiring extra forward passes or probe training.

items.title: What Shapes Brain Alignment of Large Language Models during Dialogue? Insights from Language Production and Comprehension
items.abstract: Brain alignment of large language models (LLMs) offers a way to investigate representational similarities between LLMs and the human brain during language processing. While previous studies have mainly focused on passive language comprehension, little is known about such alignment during dialogue, in which speakers engage in both language production and comprehension. In this study, using fMRI data collected during dialogue, we examine brain alignment during language production and comprehension across LLM layers and brain regions. We assess its association with the intrinsic dimension (ID) of LLM representations and the contributions of several interpretable linguistic and communicative features. Our results reveal distinct patterns of brain alignment between production and comprehension, as well as strong associations with ID in brain regions associated with each processing mode. Furthermore, we show that the contributions of linguistic and communicative features also vary across processing modes, LLM layers, and brain regions.

items.title: When Can You Trust an Agent's Own Verifier? Stress-Testing Counterfactual Rationale Verification Under Search Pressure and Oracle Access
items.abstract: Automated agent design increasingly trusts a single score to decide whether a change is an improvement -- but a score optimized aggressively enough ceases to measure what it was meant to. When an agent also explains its design, that explanation is a second signal we can check without human labels: negate each stated claim, re-run, and observe whether performance drops. We ask whether such a verifier stays reliable once an agent optimizes against it. Our contribution is not a new verifier but a way to stress-test one: a pressure ratio $ρ$ measuring how much the verifier steers the agent's search, and four falsifiable probes covering four failure modes -- giving no signal, being too weak to matter, being gamed by stating fewer claims, and being queried before the agent commits. We apply the test to our own verifier, the Rationale Consistency Score (RCS), inside an LLM agent that designs machine-learning pipelines, with one generator model, six tasks, and three seeds. First, in our prior configuration the verifier barely affects the search objective ($ρ\ll 1$), partly because of an accuracy gate, so its robustness had not been tested; it still shapes the reported artifact through a final-selection tie-break that $ρ$ does not register. Second, a capability control shows the agent shortens its claim lists when instructed, yet search does not, even at $ρ$ over 100 times the prior level; since feedback omits claim volume and horizons are short, this null result is largely structural rather than evidence of robustness. Third, when the agent can probe the verifier before committing, it keeps claims that pass while held-out faithfulness falls -- a decline invisible to in-loop metrics, though partly confounded by how RCS scores small pipelines. We offer these as preliminary evidence and propose a reporting standard: audit a verifier with $ρ$ and these probes before trusting it.

items.title: When is travel-health AI inference transportable? Mobility-conditioned admissibility for cross-border disease risk and decision support
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Artificial intelligence is increasingly used for infectious disease surveillance, traveller risk assessment, outbreak forecasting and decision support. Travel creates a distinctive transportability problem because people move between epidemiological, geographic, climatic and healthcare contexts in which the conditions supporting an inference may change rapidly. METHODS: This conceptual/theoretical methodological-development study was informed by a targeted narrative review of travel medicine, infectious disease surveillance, human mobility, border health, mass gatherings, antimicrobial resistance and health-AI validation literature. RESULTS: We develop a mobility-conditioned admissibility framework that treats travel as movement across origin, transit, destination and return regimes. Interpretation is conditioned on mobility state, epidemiological regime, exposure history, time-dependent constraints and clinical or biological constraints. Five proposed operational states are retained: supported inference, conditionally transportable inference, active monitoring, restricted interpretation and withholding. The framework also distinguishes low probability from infeasibility and requires preservation of rare but epidemiologically feasible events. CONCLUSIONS: Model availability and conventional predictive validity do not establish inferential transportability across changing travel contexts. Mobility-conditioned admissibility provides a complementary use-boundary layer for travel health AI by making cross-regime support explicit before outputs are interpreted or released. Its incremental value requires prospective evaluation against calibrated uncertainty, external validation and dataset-shift monitoring.
